facts.fact: The Government Complex Sejong was built to move South Korea's central government agencies out of the Seoul metropolitan area, for decentralisation and more balanced development.
facts.quote: The Government Complex Sejong (Korean: 정부세종청사) is a government building built to create a multi-functional administrative city by relocating central administrative agencies to the non-metropolitan area for the purpose of decentralization, balanced development, and overcrowding in the metropolitan area.

facts.fact: Inside, departments and individuals are not separated, and desks are arranged together regardless of rank.
facts.quote: There is no separation between departments or individuals, and desks are arranged together regardless of position.

facts.fact: Its roof garden, inspired by the Korean traditional game Sunseongnori, links 15 buildings and was listed by Guinness World Records in 2016 as the world's largest, at 3.6 km.
facts.quote: There is a roof garden inspired by Sunseongnori, Korea's Traditional Play, it was listed in the Guinness Book of World Records in 2016 as the world's largest (3.6 km) garden with 15 buildings connected.

facts.fact: The complex has seven storeys and one basement on a 213,000 m² plot.
facts.quote: The complex, on a 213,000-square-metre (2,290,000 sq ft) plot of land, has seven stories and one basement.

facts.fact: Construction started in December 2008 and was finished in stages, the last in November 2014.
facts.quote: In December 2008, construction for the Sejong Government Complex started. After level 1 of the construction was completed in November 2012, level 2 was finished in November 2013, and finished construction in November 2014.

facts.fact: It has an employee lounge, multipurpose communication spaces and conference rooms.
facts.quote: It is equipped with an employee lounge, multipurpose communication space, and conference room.

facts.fact: Seonyudo Park is an ecological park that covers the whole of Seonyudo, a small island in the Han River in Seoul, beside the Yanghwa Bridge.
facts.quote: There is a Seonyudo park all over the island. The total area of the island is 0.11 km2. Seonyudo Park is an ecological park that meets the Yanghwa Bridge.

facts.fact: The island was once a small hill, Seonyubong, which disappeared entirely when the Yanghwa Bridge was built in 1962–65.
facts.quote: With the construction of the Yanghwa Bridge from June 1962 to January 1965, Seonyubong completely disappeared.

facts.fact: From 1978 to 2000 the island held a water filtration plant supplying tap water to south-western Seoul.
facts.quote: From 1978 to 2000, Seonyudo was used as a water filtration plant to supply tap water to the southwestern part of Seoul.

facts.fact: The filtration plant closed in December 2000 and the park opened on its site on 26 April 2002.
facts.quote: In December 2000, Seonyudo water filtration plant was closed and then a park was set up. On April 26, 2002, it opened as a public park, Seonyudo Park.

facts.fact: The old filtration plant was recycled into a water purification garden that cleans water with aquatic plants and supplies the park.
facts.quote: Water purification plant: Water purification plants were made by recycling past Seonyudo water filtration plant. It uses aquatic plants to purify water and supplies water to various facilities in the park.

facts.fact: In the Garden of Green Columns, the columns of the old reservoir were kept as a trace of the past, with ivy growing on them.
facts.quote: Garden of green column: The garden is where the columns are left to show the vestiges of the reservoir that used to hold water and an ivy is growing on the columns.

facts.fact: The Seoul National University Museum of Art was designed by Rem Koolhaas; its outer skin of U-glass shows the steel trusses that carry it.
facts.quote: The SNUMoA was designed by Rem Koolhaas. The structure's exterior is made of U-glass which reveals the underlying structural steel framed trusses.

facts.fact: The building uses its sloping site and is cantilevered from a concrete core, so it appears light and floating.
facts.quote: The building is located on sloping site which the architect utilized in the final design. The museum is cantilevered on a concrete core, thus giving the appearance of lightness and floating in space.

facts.fact: The museum has four programme areas (operations, education, exhibition and library), and the slope gives the auditorium its raked seating.
facts.quote: The museum is divided into four basic program areas: Operations, Educational, Exhibition, and Library. The slope of the building benefits the auditorium which has ramped seating.

facts.fact: The museum was proposed in 1995 by Professor Jong-Sang Lee, with funding promised by the Samsung Foundation of Culture.
facts.quote: 1995 Prof. Jong-Sang Lee proposes the establishment of the MoA and the Samsung Cultural foundation promises to fund the creation of the museum.

facts.fact: The structure was built in 2004–05 and the museum opened on 8 June 2006.
facts.quote: 2004 Construction of the structure begins. 2005 The construction of the structure is completed. 2006 The Museum of Art opens on June 8.

facts.fact: It regularly shows students' work alongside work by Korean and international designers and artists.
facts.quote: The SNUMoA holds regular exhibitions of students’ work as well as work from international and domestic designers and artists.

facts.fact: The Galileo Galilei Planetarium stands in Parque Tres de Febrero in the Palermo district of Buenos Aires.
facts.quote: The Galileo Galilei planetarium, commonly known as Planetario, is located in Parque Tres de Febrero in the Palermo district of Buenos Aires, Argentina.

facts.fact: Building began in 1962 under architect Enrique Jan, and the planetarium was inaugurated on 20 December 1966.
facts.quote: Construction began under the direction of architect Enrique Jan in 1962, and it was inaugurated on December 20, 1966.

facts.fact: The idea of a planetarium for Buenos Aires took shape in 1958, through an agreement between councillor José Luis Peña and the city's culture secretary, Aldo Cocca.
facts.quote: The idea that Buenos Aires should have a planetarium began to take shape in 1958 by an agreement between Socialist Councilman José Luis Peña and the municipal Secretary of Culture, Dr. Aldo Cocca.

facts.fact: The building has five floors, six staircases and a 20 m round hall with 360 seats under a hemispherical dome lined with reflective aluminium.
facts.quote: The building has five floors, six staircases and a 20 metres (66 ft) diameter room with 360 seats. The inside of the 20 m semispherical dome is covered with reflective aluminium.

facts.fact: It officially opened to the public on 5 April 1968.
facts.quote: The facility was officially opened to the public on April 5, 1968.

facts.fact: It stands on the site from which the Buenos Aires Football Club and Buenos Aires Cricket Club were evicted in the late 1940s.
facts.quote: The planetarium was built in the same exact site from where the Buenos Aires Football Club and the Buenos Aires Cricket Club were evicted in the very late 1940s.

facts.fact: Its collection includes a piece of lunar rock brought back by Apollo 11 and given to the planetarium by Richard Nixon.
facts.quote: The museum has a piece of lunar rock which was brought back to Earth by the Apollo 11 mission and gifted to the planetarium by Richard Nixon.

facts.fact: Estádio Serra Dourada is a football stadium in Goiânia, Brazil, opened on 9 March 1975 and designed by Paulo Mendes da Rocha.
facts.quote: Estádio Serra Dourada is a football stadium inaugurated on March 9, 1975 in Goiânia, Goiás, Brazil. It was designed by the Pritzker Prize-winning Brazilian architect Paulo Mendes da Rocha.

facts.fact: The stadium is owned by the government of Goiás state and mainly hosts state matches.
facts.quote: The stadium is owned by the Goiás state Government and primarily hosts state matches.

facts.fact: The city's three main clubs use their own grounds for most games but move to Serra Dourada for derbies and other big matches.
facts.quote: Vila Nova, Goias Esporte Clube and Atlético Goianiense all have their own stadiums which they use for most league games, but for derbies and other big games they move to the Serra Dourada.

facts.fact: It was one of the venues of the 1989 Copa América.
facts.quote: Serra Dourada was completed in 1975 and was inaugurated on March 9 of that same year. It was one of the venues of the 1989 Copa América.

facts.fact: Its record attendance, 79,610, was set at the opening match.
facts.quote: The inauguration match also marked the stadium's attendance record, at 79,610.

facts.fact: Cuba's National Art Schools, now the Instituto Superior de Arte, are considered by historians among the most outstanding architectural achievements of the Cuban Revolution.
facts.quote: Cuba's National Art Schools (Escuelas Nacionales de Arte, now known as the Instituto Superior de Arte) are considered by historians to be among the most outstanding architectural achievements of the Cuban Revolution.

facts.fact: The organic brick and terracotta buildings with Catalan vaults stand on a former country club in Cubanacán, western Havana; Fidel Castro and Che Guevara founded the schools in 1961.
facts.quote: These innovative, organic Catalan-vaulted brick and terra-cotta structures were built on the site of a former country club in the far western Havana suburb of Cubanacán, which was once considered to be Havana's "Beverly Hills", The schools were conceived and founded by Fidel Castro and Che Guevara in 1961, and they reflect the utopian optimism and revolutionary exuberance of the early years of the Cuban Revolution.

facts.fact: The design, by Ricardo Porro, Roberto Gottardi and Vittorio Garatti, ran counter to the International Style that dominated at the time.
facts.quote: The design of the National Art Schools, created by Ricardo Porro, Roberto Gottardi, and Vittorio Garatti, ran counter to the dominant International Style of the time.

facts.fact: Because the US embargo made steel rebar and Portland cement costly, the architects used local brick and terracotta tile and built with the Catalan vault for its organic forms.
facts.quote: The US embargo against Cuba, begun in 1960, had made the importation of rebar and Portland cement very costly. The architects therefore decided to use locally produced brick and terracotta tile, and for the constructive system they would use the Catalan vault with its potential for organic form.

facts.fact: The academy held five schools: Modern Dance, Plastic Arts, Dramatic Arts, Music and Ballet.
facts.quote: There were five art schools within the academy: the School of Modern Dance, the School of Plastic Arts, the School of Dramatic Arts, the School of Music, and the School of Ballet.

facts.fact: Garatti's School of Music is a winding ribbon 330 m long that follows the contours of the land down towards the river.
facts.quote: The School of Music is constructed as a serpentine ribbon 330 meters long, embedded in and traversing the contours of the landscape approaching the river.

facts.fact: In July 1965 the schools were declared finished, complete or not, and construction stopped.
facts.quote: In July 1965, the National Art Schools were declared finished in their various stages of completion and incompletion, and construction came to a halt.

facts.fact: In November 2010 the Cuban government recognised the schools as national monuments.
facts.quote: In November 2010, the National Art Schools were officially recognized as national monuments by the Cuban Government, and they are currently being considered for inclusion on the World Heritage list of sites which have "outstanding universal value" to the world.

facts.fact: Zaha Hadid built the Sheikh Zayed Bridge between 1997 and 2010; named after Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, it links Abu Dhabi island with the mainland and the airport.
facts.quote: Between 1997 and 2010, she constructed a much more ambitious bridge, the Sheikh Zayed Bridge, which honors Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, between the island of Abu Dhabi and the mainland of Abu Dhabi, as well as to the Abu Dhabi International Airport.

facts.fact: Both the bridge's form and its slowly changing coloured lighting were designed to suggest movement.
facts.quote: Both the design of the bridge and the lighting, consisting of gradually changing colours, were designed to give the impression of movement.

facts.fact: The bridge's silhouette is a wave, with a main arch 235 m long rising 60 m above the water.
facts.quote: The silhouette of the bridge is a wave, with a principal arch 235 metres long, standing 60 metres above the water.

facts.fact: It carries four lanes and pedestrian walkways over a total length of 842 m.
facts.quote: The total span of four lanes is 842 metres (2,762 feet) long, and also includes pedestrian walkways.

facts.fact: It was inaugurated on 25 November 2010 by UAE President Sheikh Khalifa.
facts.quote: The bridge was inaugurated on 25 November 2010, by the late UAE President Sheikh Khalifa.

facts.fact: It was the third bridge joining Abu Dhabi island to the mainland, after the Maqta and Mussafah bridges.
facts.quote: It is on an island less than 250 metres (820 ft) from the mainland and is joined to the mainland by the Maqta and Mussafah Bridges. A third, Sheikh Zayed Bridge, designed by Zaha Hadid, opened in late 2010.

facts.fact: Lusail Stadium, the largest stadium in Qatar and the Middle East by capacity, was one of eight built for the 2022 FIFA World Cup and hosted its final.
facts.quote: Owned by the Qatar Football Association, it is the largest stadium in Qatar and the Middle East by capacity; one of eight stadiums built for the 2022 FIFA World Cup, it hosted the 2022 FIFA World Cup final game between Argentina and France on 18 December 2022.

facts.fact: Construction began on 11 April 2017.
facts.quote: Construction began on 11 April 2017.

facts.fact: It was inaugurated on 9 September 2022 with the Lusail Super Cup.
facts.quote: Lusail Stadium was inaugurated on 9 September 2022 with the Lusail Super Cup game.

facts.fact: It was built by a joint venture of HBK Contracting and China Railway Construction Corporation.
facts.quote: The stadium was built as a joint venture by HBK Contracting and the China Railway Construction Corporation.

facts.fact: Like the other World Cup stadiums, it is cooled using solar power and is claimed to have a zero carbon footprint.
facts.quote: Like the other stadiums that planned the 2022 World Cup, the Lusail Stadium is cooled using solar power and is claimed to have zero carbon footprint.

facts.fact: After the World Cup it was meant to shrink to 40,000 seats, with the rest of the building turned into community space with shops, cafés, sports and education facilities and a clinic.
facts.quote: Following the World Cup, it is expected to be reconfigured into a 40,000-seat stadium. Excess seating will be removed and other parts of the building repurposed as a community space with shops, cafés, athletic and education facilities, and a health clinic.

facts.fact: The planned cut from 88,966 to 40,000 seats had still not happened as of December 2025.
facts.quote: As of 2022 it was the second largest football stadium in Asia, with a plan to eventually reduce capacity from 88,966 to 40,000. However, as of December 2025 this has yet to happen.

facts.fact: It received a five-star GSAS sustainability rating for its design and construction on 16 August 2022.
facts.quote: Like other stadiums constructed for the 2022 FIFA World Cup, Lusail Stadium received a five-star rating on 16 August 2022 for its design and construction from the GSAS.

facts.fact: Qatar University is a public research university on the northern outskirts of Doha, and the only public university in Qatar.
facts.quote: Qatar University (Arabic: جامعة قطر; transliterated: Jami'at Qatar) is a public research university located on the northern outskirts of Doha, Qatar. It is the only public university in the country.

facts.fact: It was founded in 1973 as a College of Education, by decree of the Emir of Qatar.
facts.quote: The institution was established as the College of Education by a decree from the Emir of Qatar in 1973.

facts.fact: The founding of new colleges, ending with Business and Economics in 1985, led to a large expansion of the campus overseen by Kamal El Kafrawi.
facts.quote: This was followed by the establishment of the College of Business & Economics in 1985. The new colleges prompted a large expansion of the university campus, which was overseen Kamal El Kafrawi.

facts.fact: The campus is in the Al Tarfa district on the northern edge of Doha, about 16 km from the city centre.
facts.quote: Qatar University is situated on the northern edge of Doha in the district of Al Tarfa, approximately 16 kilometers from the city center.

facts.fact: Women make up about 70% of the students and have their own facilities and classrooms.
facts.quote: Women make up approximately 70% of the student population, and are provided their own set of facilities and classrooms.

facts.fact: King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has four passenger terminals, each with eight air bridges, plus a mosque and parking for 11,600 cars.
facts.quote: This airport consists of four passenger terminals with eight aero-bridges each, a mosque, and parking facilities for 11,600 vehicles.

facts.fact: Planning and site selection for a replacement for Riyadh's old airport began in 1974.
facts.quote: In 1974, the planning and site selection of a replacement airport for the old airport began as part of the Airports Development Program.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1976; the airport, designed by Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum (HOK), was opened by King Fahd on 16 November 1983.
facts.quote: In 1976, construction of King Khalid International Airport (KKIA) began. It was designed by architectural practice Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum, was opened by HRH King Fahd on 16 November 1983, and opened for scheduled flights on 5 December of the same year.

facts.fact: Terminals 1 to 4 date from the 1983 opening and are joined by three linking buildings, each 168 m long.
facts.quote: Terminals 1 to 4 were built when the airport was opened in November 1983. They are connected to each other by means of three linking buildings, each 168 metres (551 ft 2 in) long.

facts.fact: Each of the original terminals is triangular in plan, with a base area of 47,500 m².
facts.quote: Each terminal is triangular in plan, with a base area of 47,500 square metres (511,000 sq ft).

facts.fact: The Royal Pavilion is also triangular, with a roof of 33 arched sections rising to 30 m, and glass walls that light the interior.
facts.quote: Like the passenger terminals, the Royal Pavilion has a triangular plan, with a roof composed of 33 arched sections rising to a high point 30 metres (98 ft 5 in) above the ground level. Glass walls and windows illuminate the interior of the building.

facts.fact: The airport mosque, also by HOK and built in 1983, is hexagonal in plan and covers 5,600 m².
facts.quote: Built in 1983, the mosque covers an area of 5,600 m2 (60,000 sq ft) in a hexagonal plan and was designed by the US-based architectural firm HOK.

facts.fact: The mosque's stained glass, by British artist Brian Clarke, is considered the largest and most technically advanced stained glass project of the modern period.
facts.quote: The Royal Mosque was designed with a significant programme of integral art; the stained glass, by British architectural artist Brian Clarke, was a landmark work in the history of the medium, considered to be the largest and technically most advanced stained glass project of the modern period.

facts.fact: Maraya Concert Hall in AlUla was designed and built by Giò Forma Studio and Black Engineering for the concerts of the Winter at Tantora festival; its outer walls are covered in mirrors, and "maraya" is Arabic for "mirrors".
facts.quote: The concerts were performed in Maraya Concert Hall, which was newly design and constructed by Giò Forma Studio and Black Engineering for this purpose, and whose external walls are covered with mirrors, maraya being the Arabic word for 'mirrors'.

facts.fact: On 26 December 2019 it set a Guinness World Record as the largest mirrored building in the world, with 9,740 m² of mirrored facade.
facts.quote: On 26 December 2019, Maraya Concert Hall set a Guinness World Record for the largest mirrored building in the world, in which it was covered by 9,740 square metres (104,800 sq ft) of mirrored façade.

facts.fact: It is counted among AlUla's most popular sites, alongside the Old Town, Hegra and Elephant Rock.
facts.quote: Its most popular sites are: al-Ula Old town, Oasis Heritage Trail, Hegra UNESCO Heritage Site, Dadan, Jabal Ikmah, Jabal AlFil (Elephant Rock), Harrarat Viewpoint or Maraya Concert Hall.

facts.fact: The Holiday Inn Beirut was built in 1971–74 for developer Abdal Mohsin Kattan, designed by French architect André Wogenscky with Lebanese architect Maurice Hindié.
facts.quote: The hotel was constructed between 1971 and 1974 by Lebanese developer Abdal Mohsin Kattan and designed by French architect André Wogenscky, working with Lebanese architect Maurice Hindié.

facts.fact: The 26-storey hotel had 400 rooms, a nightclub on the 25th floor and a revolving restaurant on top, and was part of the mixed-use St. Charles City Center with a cinema, offices and shops.
facts.quote: The 26-storey hotel included a revolving restaurant on the top floor, a nightclub on the 25th floor, and 400 guest rooms. It was part of a mixed-use complex known as St. Charles City Center, including a cinema, offices, shops, restaurants, a supermarket.

facts.fact: It opened in 1974 at the height of Beirut's boom and ran normally for only a year before the Lebanese Civil War began in 1975.
facts.quote: The Holiday Inn opened in 1974, at the height of Beirut's economic boom, when the city was the glamorous tourist center of the Middle East. The Holiday Inn operated normally for only a year before the Lebanese Civil War broke out in 1975.

facts.fact: From October 1975 the tower was the focus of the Battle of the Hotels, in which militias fought for the city's tall luxury hotels.
facts.quote: The hotel became the focal point of a war zone beginning on October 25, 1975, in a months-long conflict known as the Battle of the Hotels, as over 25,000 combatants from pro-Palestinian and Christian militias fought for control of a group of towering luxury hotels including the Holiday Inn and the adjacent Phoenicia Inter-Continental, resulting in over 1,000 deaths (many of those who died were thrown from the top of the Holiday Inn) and 2,000 injuries.

facts.fact: After the battle, scavengers stripped the hotel down to its concrete skeleton.
facts.quote: After the battle, the ruined hotel was stripped to its concrete skeleton by scavengers.

facts.fact: Its two owners disagree: the Lebanese half-owner wants to renovate it into condominiums, while the Kuwaiti half-owner wants to demolish it and build a new tower.
facts.quote: The Lebanese company that owns half of it, Compagnie Immobiliere Libanaise, wants to renovate it and convert it to condos, while the Kuwaiti group that owns the other half wants to demolish it and construct a new tower on the site.

facts.fact: The ruin and the ground around it are a military zone controlled by the Lebanese Army, which restricts public access.
facts.quote: Due to its strategic location in Beirut's city centre, the ruined hotel and its immediate surrounding ground level areas have been declared a military zone, and the structure is under the control of the Lebanese Army, which currently restricts access to civilians.

facts.fact: In 1959 an arched Monument to the Unknown Soldier, designed by Rifat Chadirji, was put up in Baghdad's Firdos Square as a modern version of the ancient arch of Ctesiphon.
facts.quote: In 1959, an arched monument to the Unknown Soldier was erected in Baghdad's Firdos Square. It was designed by Iraqi architect, Rifat Chadirji, and was a modern adaption of the arch of Ctesiphon in the ancient capital of the Parthian Empire.

facts.fact: It commemorated the wars of independence fought against the monarchy imposed by the British.
facts.quote: In 1959, he was commissioned to construct The Monument to the Unknown Soldier in Baghdad's Firdos Square to commemorate the wars of independence fought against the British imposed monarchy.

facts.fact: Chadirji's sketches show that the design represents a mother bending to pick up her martyred child.
facts.quote: Sketches of the design found at the Institute of Fine Arts in Baghdad, reveal the inspiration for the design which represents a mother bending over to pick up her martyred child.

facts.fact: It is described as a simple, symbolic, modernist structure.
facts.quote: Described as a simple, symbolic, modernist structure, a comparison between the original and its later replacement illustrates the increasing level of abstraction and sophistication in Iraqi art during the period.

facts.fact: It was removed in the early 1980s to make way for a statue of Saddam Hussein.
facts.quote: The original was removed from al-Fardous Square to make way for a statue of Saddam Hussein in the early 1980s.

facts.fact: The Izvestia newspaper headquarters, designed by Grigori Barkhin, is an example of the modern offices built for the mass press in 1920s Moscow.
facts.quote: Modern offices for the mass press were also popular, such as the Izvestia headquarters. This was built in 1926–7 and designed by Grigori Barkhin

facts.fact: The Constructivist Izvestia Building by Grigory Barkhin (1925–27) on Pushkin Square is one of three modernist buildings Tverskaya Street gained between the Revolution and the rise of Stalinist architecture.
facts.quote: Between the Russian Revolution of 1917 and the rise of Stalinist architecture in mid-1930s, the street acquired three modernist buildings - constructivist Izvestia Building by Grigory Barkhin (1925–1927, Pushkin Square), Central Telegraph Building (1927–1929, 7 Tverskaya), a modernist masterpiece by Ivan Rerberg, and a stern "black cube" of the Lenin Institute in Tverskaya Square (1926) by Stepan Chernyshyov.

facts.fact: The border checkpoint at Sarpi is one of several public and infrastructure projects in Georgia by Jürgen Mayer H.'s firm.
facts.quote: Recent national and international projects include Metropol Parasol, the redevelopment of the Plaza de la Encarnación in Seville, Spain; the Court of Justice in Hasselt, Belgium; Pavilion KA300, built in celebration of Karlsruhe's 300th jubilee, and several public and infrastructural projects in Georgia—for example, an airport in Mestia, the border checkpoint in Sarpi, and three rest stops along the highway in Gori and Lochini.

facts.fact: The firm dates the Sarpi checkpoint to 2010–2011.
facts.quote: Border Checkpoint, Sarpi, Georgia, 2010–2011

facts.fact: The Kazakhstan Central Concert Hall in Astana was designed by Italian architect Manfredi Nicoletti and opened by President Nursultan Nazarbayev on Independence Day, 15 December 2009.
facts.quote: It was designed by Italian architect Manfredi Nicoletti and inaugurated by the President of Kazakhstan, Nursultan Nazarbayev, on the nation's Independence Day, 15 December, in 2009.

facts.fact: The building's shape suggests the movement of a flower's petals.
facts.quote: The building’s shape evokes the dynamism of a flower's petals.

facts.fact: Its outer structure is a series of curved, inclined concrete walls clad in back-painted blue glass, which shield the interior from Astana's harsh weather.
facts.quote: The building's external structure comprises a series of curved inclined walls made of concrete with a blue back painted glass panels cladding. Those structures protect the building's interior functions from Astana’s harsh weather.

facts.fact: A 30 m high foyer of over 3,000 m² is meant as an indoor public square that people can use all year.
facts.quote: The building features a thirty-meter-high foyer which extends over 3.000 square meters, which is intended to create an urban-scale internal public square that could welcome the citizens of Astana throughout the entire year.

facts.fact: The main hall seats 3,500 and can host classical and pop concerts, ballet and conferences because its acoustics are adjustable.
facts.quote: The main Concert hall for 3,500 seats is one of the biggest of its kind and is capable of hosting a multitude of different events, from classical to pop music, ballet and conferences thanks to its acoustic flexibility.

facts.fact: The acoustics are adjusted with curtains and a special "black-hole" false ceiling that absorbs most reflections.
facts.quote: This flexibility is produced by a system of acoustic curtains and a special false ceiling design called a black-hole, which absorbs most of the acoustic reflections of the hall.

facts.fact: Two smaller halls, of 400 and 200 seats, can host chamber music, cinema and conferences.
facts.quote: The two smaller halls, of 400 and 200 seats respectively, have been designed to be flexible enough to host chamber music as well as cinema and conferences.

facts.fact: The Palace of the Republic in Almaty is used for concerts, festivals and other cultural events.
facts.quote: It is intended for concerts, festivals and other cultural events.

facts.fact: It stands on Abai Square, at the crossing of Dostyq and Abai avenues.
facts.quote: The building is located at the Abai Square in cross road section of Dostyq and Abai Avenue.

facts.fact: Built in 1970 as the Lenin Palace of Culture, it opened for the centenary of Lenin's birth.
facts.quote: Built in 1970, previously named as the Lenin Palace of Culture, was opened during the celebration of the 100th anniversary of the birth of Vladimir Lenin.

facts.fact: Its tent-like roof rests on eight concrete pillars; the outer walls stop short of the roof, so it seems to float.
facts.quote: The "Tent" design of the roof rests on the eight concrete pillars and walls of the building envelope, not reaching the roof, give the impression of it floating in the air.

facts.fact: The 13 m high main lobby has a white chandelier, and the stair railings and marble floors of the entrance hall and lobby draw on national motifs.
facts.quote: The main lobby with a height 13 m is decorated with snow-white chandelier. The decoration of the entrance hall and the lobby was reflected national character structures such as figure stairway fence lines, marble floors, etc.

facts.fact: The stage is 48 m wide and 18 m deep; after reconstruction the hall seats 2,567, down from 3,000.
facts.quote: The width of the stage is 48 meters, with the depth of 18 m. After the reconstruction, the seats in auditorium was 2567 while before there were 3000.

facts.fact: The Alma-Ata Declaration on primary health care was adopted at a meeting held in the palace in 1978.
facts.quote: The palace was also place for International Primary Health Care meeting where the Alma-Ata Declaration was adopted in 1978.

facts.fact: It was listed as a monument of history, culture, town planning and architecture of national significance on 21 March 2008.
facts.quote: On March 21, 2008 the status “Monument of history, culture, town planning and architecture of republican significance” was awarded.

facts.fact: The Tallinn Song Festival Grounds host the Estonian Song Festival, held every five years.
facts.quote: The Tallinn Song Festival Grounds (Estonian: Lauluväljak) are the grounds on which the Estonian Song Festival "Laulupidu" is held every five years.

facts.fact: The present arched stage was built in 1959, designed by Henno Sepmann with Alar Kotli and Endel Paalmann.
facts.quote: The new and current arched stage was built in 1959 to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the Estonian SSR in the upcoming year. It was designed by architect Henno Sepmann together with Alar Kotli and Endel Paalmann.

facts.fact: The first stage on the site, in Kadriorg, was built in 1928 to a design by Karl Burman and held 15,000 performers.
facts.quote: The first stage on its current location between Narva Road and Pirita Road in Kadriorg was built in 1928 for the 9th Estonian Song Festival. It was designed by Karl Burman and provided space for 15,000 performers.

facts.fact: The new stage was first used for the 15th Estonian Song Festival in 1960.
facts.quote: The 15th Estonian Song Festival in 1960 was celebrated on the new stage.

facts.fact: The stage was meant for over 15,000 singers, but it can also be used the other way round, with the performance in front and the audience sitting on the stage.
facts.quote: The stage was meant to hold over 15,000 singers but the reverse also became possible, with the performance taking place in front of the stage and audience sitting on the stage.

facts.fact: A 42 m fire tower stands on the north side of the stage and is used during the song festivals.
facts.quote: On the northern side of the song stage is the 42m high fire tower, which is used during the Estonian Song Festivals.

facts.fact: In 1988 Estonians gathered here to sing patriotic songs in the Singing Revolution that led to the end of Soviet rule.
facts.quote: In 1988, Estonians gathered at the Tallinn Song Festival Grounds, to sing patriotic hymns in what became known as the Singing Revolution that led to the overthrow of Soviet rule.

facts.fact: The airport in Mestia is one of several public and infrastructure projects in Georgia by Jürgen Mayer H.'s firm.
facts.quote: Recent national and international projects include Metropol Parasol, the redevelopment of the Plaza de la Encarnación in Seville, Spain; the Court of Justice in Hasselt, Belgium; Pavilion KA300, built in celebration of Karlsruhe's 300th jubilee, and several public and infrastructural projects in Georgia—for example, an airport in Mestia, the border checkpoint in Sarpi, and three rest stops along the highway in Gori and Lochini.

facts.fact: The firm's project list dates Queen Tamar Airport in Mestia to 2010.
facts.quote: Queen Tamar Airport, Mestia, Georgia, 2010.

facts.fact: The Russian State Scientific Center for Robotics and Technical Cybernetics (RTC) is a St Petersburg research institute specialising in software, hardware, robotics and technical cybernetics.
facts.quote: Located in St. Petersburg, it specializes in software and hardware development, and in robotics and technical cybernetics.

facts.fact: It began as a design bureau formed at the St Petersburg Polytechnic University in 1968 and became the RTC in June 1981.
facts.quote: Special design bureau for technical cybernetics was formed on the base of Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic University on January 29, 1968. In June 1981, the bureau was transformed into the RTC.

facts.fact: In 1986–87 the institute built mobile robots for radiation reconnaissance and clean-up after the Chernobyl accident.
facts.quote: In 1986–1987, the institute created mobile robots for radiation reconnaissance and liquidation of Chernobyl accident consequences.

facts.fact: Lascaux IV is a full-size replica of the whole Lascaux cave.
facts.quote: Lascaux IV is the latest replica, in real scale, of the integrality of the cave of Lascaux.

facts.fact: It stands on the same hill above Montignac, 400 m from the original cave, as part of the International Centre for Parietal Art, opened in December 2016.
facts.quote: Situated on the same hill overlooking Montignac, and 400 m (440 yd) from the original site, it is part of the International Centre for Parietal Art (Centre International de l'Art Pariétal) that was inaugurated in December 2016.

facts.fact: The museum, built by Snøhetta, adds digital technology, workshops and films in display rooms next to the replica.
facts.quote: The museum, built by Snøhetta, integrates digital technology, workshops and films into adjacent display rooms.

facts.fact: It is larger and more accurate than Lascaux II, the earlier replica opened nearby in 1983.
facts.quote: A replica cave, known as Lascaux II, was opened nearby in 1983, so that visitors could still experience the paintings without damaging the originals. Since 2016 a larger and more accurate replica is displayed in Lascaux IV Centre International de l'Art Pariétal built by Snøhetta in Montignac.

facts.fact: Replicas are needed because the original cave has been closed to the public since 1963, when its condition was quickly deteriorating.
facts.quote: The original caves have been closed to the public since 1963, as their condition was quickly deteriorating, but there are now a number of replicas.

facts.fact: The Maison de l'Iran, a student residence at the Cité internationale universitaire de Paris, was designed by Heydar Ghiai and Mohsen Foroughi with André Bloc and Claude Parent.
facts.quote: Outside Iran, Ghiai and Foroughi collaborated with André Bloc and French architect Claude Parent on the Maison de l'Iran, a student residence at the Cité internationale universitaire de Paris.

facts.fact: After the Paris authorities rejected Ghiai and Foroughi's first proposal, Bloc introduced them to Parent; their joint design was completed in 1969.
facts.quote: Ghiai and Foroughi had prepared an earlier proposal for the building, but after it was not approved by the Paris authorities, Bloc introduced the architects to Parent. The collaborative design was completed in 1969.

facts.fact: It was built to give about 100 rooms to Iranian students.
facts.quote: The residence was created to provide approximately 100 rooms for Iranian students.

facts.fact: Its residential floors hang from a structure of three welded-steel frames about 38 m high.
facts.quote: Its residential floors are suspended from a macrostructure formed by three welded-steel frames about 38 metres high.

facts.fact: A large outside steel staircase was designed as a separate sculptural element.
facts.quote: A large external steel staircase was designed as a separate sculptural feature.

facts.fact: In 1972 it passed to the Cité internationale and was renamed Fondation Avicenne; it was listed as a French historic monument in 2008.
facts.quote: The building was transferred to the Cité internationale and renamed the Fondation Avicenne in 1972. It was placed on France's list of historic monuments in 2008.

facts.fact: The Fondation Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé, a non-profit recognised in 2006, preserves, restores and promotes Pathé's film heritage of more than 10,000 films.
facts.quote: The Fondation Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé, which he founded and was recognized as a non-profit organization in 2006, serves to preserve, restore, and enhance Pathé's historical heritage, which includes more than 10,000 films.

facts.fact: In February 1936 a fire destroyed all of Turin's Teatro Regio except its facade, and it stayed closed for 37 years.
facts.quote: Until February 1936, seasons of opera were presented until fire destroyed all but the facade of the Teatro Regio. It remained closed for thirty-seven years.

facts.fact: A national competition for an architect followed the fire, but because of the war and lack of money the foundation stone was only laid on 25 September 1963.
facts.quote: Following the fire, a national competition was launched to find an architect. However, with the war and the overall financial situation, the foundation stone was not laid until 25 September 1963.

facts.fact: Work began in September 1967 under architect Carlo Mollino.
facts.quote: Even then, work did not start until September 1967 under architect Carlo Mollino.

facts.fact: The rebuilt theatre, with a strikingly modern interior behind the original facade, opened on 10 April 1973 with Verdi's I vespri siciliani.
facts.quote: The rebuilt theatre, with its striking contemporary interior design but hidden behind the original facade, was inaugurated on 10 April 1973 with a production of Verdi's I vespri siciliani directed by Maria Callas and Giuseppe Di Stefano.

facts.fact: The new hall seats 1,750; it is elliptical, with a large orchestra level and 37 boxes around the edge, and an acoustic shell was added to improve the sound.
facts.quote: The new house seats 1,750 and is elliptical in shape with a large orchestra level and 37 boxes around its perimeter. An acoustic shell was added to improve its sound.

facts.fact: In the foyer, Mollino turned Piranesi's Prisons into a brutalist, curved, labyrinthine space on four levels.
facts.quote: The Teatro Regio, an important part of the monumental Piazza Castello, offers fantastic spaces in which Mollino translates Piranesi's Prisons into a brutalist, curved, labyrinthine space on four levels that constitute the foyer.

facts.fact: The outer facade uses custom-cut bricks laid in a relief of stars that seem to overlap like fish scales.
facts.quote: The building's outer facade is made with a unique brickwork pattern using custom cut bricks to create a relief of stars which seems to overlap itself continuously like fishscales.

facts.fact: The facade of the Teatro Regio is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Piedmont.
facts.quote: The facade of the Teatro Regio is one of the Piedmontese buildings that are part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.fact: Erdene Zuu, in Kharkhorin, is probably the earliest surviving Buddhist monastery in Mongolia; it dates from 1585 and is part of the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape World Heritage Site.
facts.quote: The Erdene Zuu Monastery (Mongolian: Эрдэнэ Зуу хийд, romanized: Erdene Zuu khiid) is probably the earliest surviving Buddhist monastery in Mongolia. Built in 1585, it is located in Kharkhorin, Övörkhangai Province and is now included within the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape World Heritage Site.

facts.fact: Abtai Sain Khan, ruler of the Khalkha Mongols, ordered it built in 1585 after meeting the 3rd Dalai Lama and making Tibetan Buddhism the state religion.
facts.quote: Abtai Sain Khan, ruler of the Khalkha Mongols and grandfather of Zanabazar, the first Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, ordered construction of the Erdene Zuu monastery in 1585 after his meeting with the 3rd Dalai Lama and the declaration of Tibetan Buddhism as the state religion of Mongolia.

facts.fact: It was built partly with stones from the ruins of Karakorum, the 13th-century Mongol capital nearby.
facts.quote: Stones from the nearby ruins of the thirteenth century Mongol capital of Karakorum were used in its construction.

facts.fact: The planners meant the surrounding wall to resemble a Buddhist rosary of 108 stupas, a sacred number, though this was probably never achieved.
facts.quote: Planners attempted to create a surrounding wall that resembled a Tibetan Buddhist rosary featuring 108 stupas (108 being a sacred number in Buddhism), but this objective was probably never achieved.

facts.fact: The temple walls were painted, and the Chinese-style roof was covered with green tiles.
facts.quote: The monastery's temple walls were painted, and the Chinese-style roof covered with green tiles.

facts.fact: In 1792 it had 68 temples and some 15,000 lamas.
facts.quote: This monastery is also often (wrongly) referred to as the first monastery in Mongolia and it grew into a massive establishment. In 1792, it contained 68 temples and some 15,000 lamas.

facts.fact: In 1939 the communist leader Choibalsan ordered it destroyed; three small temples and the outer wall with its stupas survived.
facts.quote: In 1939, the communist leader Khorloogiin Choibalsan ordered the monastery destroyed, as part of a political purge that destroyed hundreds of monasteries in Mongolia and killed more than ten thousand monks. Three small temples and the external wall with the stupas survived the initial onslaught.

facts.fact: After communism fell in 1990 the monastery was returned to the lamas, who restored it as a place of worship.
facts.quote: After the fall of communism in Mongolia in 1990, the monastery was turned over to the lamas. They restored Erdene Zuu as a place of worship.

facts.fact: The Kauchuk Factory Club is a Russian avant-garde public building of 1927–29 by Konstantin Melnikov, on Plyushchikha Street in Moscow's Khamovniki district.
facts.quote: Kauchuk Factory Club (Russian: Клуб завода «Каучук») is a 1927-1929 russian avant-garde public building designed by Konstantin Melnikov, located in Khamovniki District of Moscow, Russia on the edge of Devichye Pole park and medical campus at 64, Plyshikha Street.

facts.fact: It was built for the Kauchuk rubber factory, which moved to Moscow from Riga in 1915.
facts.quote: Kauchuk rubber factory, originally based in Riga, relocated to Khamovniki in Moscow in 1915, threatened by German offensive, and was considerably expanded afterwards.

facts.fact: Building the club was part of a 1920s nationwide drive to replace religion with more suitable entertainment.
facts.quote: Construction of a club was part of a 1920s nationwide drive to replace religion with more appropriate entertainment.

facts.fact: Melnikov argued that a club should not be a stern temple but a place workers would run to by choice, showing what the new everyday life could be.
facts.quote: Melnikov theorized that "Club is not a stern temple of some deity. We must attain such an atmosphere, that we would not need to drag a worker in. He would run there himself, past his home and past his pub... the club, if it succeeds, will show what the new private life is all about"

facts.fact: Melnikov's clubs use bold outside stairs: building codes required wide inside staircases for fire escape, so he linked the main halls to outside galleries to save interior space.
facts.quote: One common feature of his clubs – bold use of exterior stairs – is actually a consequence of 1920s building codes that required wide internal staircase for fire evacuation. Melnikov, in an attempt to save interior space, connected the main halls to exterior galleries, which was not regulated by the code.

facts.fact: Like other 1920s buildings it has been threatened with demolition, which preservationists had managed to delay as of March 2007.
facts.quote: The club, like all 1920s buildings, is under threat of demolition. As of March, 2007, preservationists succeeded to delay demolition.

facts.fact: The interiors have been lost to careless renovation, and the original windows replaced with modern frames of the wrong size.
facts.quote: However, its interiors are lost to indiscriminate renovation, original windows are replaced with improperly-sized modern frames.

facts.fact: The Kyiv Crematorium in Memory Park at Baikove Cemetery is a landmark of neomodernist architecture whose farewell halls take the form of opened petals or portals.
facts.quote: The Wall of Memory stands in Memory Park next to a landmark of neomodernist architecture — the Kyiv Crematorium, whose halls of farewell take the form of opened petals or portals.

facts.fact: The crematorium and park were designed by architect Avraam Miletsky with the artists Ada Rybachuk and Volodymyr Melnychenko.
facts.quote: The crematorium and surrounding park were designed by architect Avraam Miletsky in collaboration with the monumental artists Ada Rybachuk and Volodymyr Melnychenko.

facts.fact: Rybachuk and Melnychenko made the park's Wall of Memory between 1968 and 1981; in January 1982, when it was nearly finished, Soviet authorities ordered it covered with concrete on ideological grounds.
facts.quote: Created between 1968 and 1981 by the artists Ada Rybachuk and Volodymyr Melnychenko within the Memory Park memorial complex, the work was nearly finished when, in January 1982, Soviet authorities ordered it covered with concrete on ideological grounds.

facts.fact: The relief was 213 m long and 4.5 to 16 m high, over 2,000 m² in all, and has been described as the largest bas-relief in Europe.
facts.quote: The high-relief was 213 metres long and ranged in height from 4.5 to 16 metres, covering more than 2,000 square metres in total — described as the largest bas-relief in Europe.

facts.fact: The wall was built on a retaining wall that holds the soil around Memory Park, turning an engineering element into the centrepiece of the complex.
facts.quote: The Wall of Memory was built on a retaining wall installed to stabilise the soil around Memory Park. The artists transformed this engineering element into the centrepiece of the entire complex.

facts.fact: The grey concrete forms were meant to be coloured with encaustic, pigment mixed with beeswax.
facts.quote: The grey forms were intended to be coloured using encaustic — an ancient technique combining pigments with beeswax.

facts.fact: In May 1982 the reliefs were buried under liquid concrete, and the work became known as the "Wall of Oblivion".
facts.quote: In May 1982, the bas-reliefs were buried under tons of liquid concrete, transforming the work into what has since been called the "Wall of Oblivion".

facts.fact: In May 2018 a first fragment, about six square metres, was uncovered beside the path to the crematorium.
facts.quote: On 18 May 2018, as part of Kyiv Art Week, a fragment of the Wall titled "Defence of the Fatherland" was unveiled along the path to the crematorium; about six square metres of relief were cleared.

facts.fact: The Tbilisi Service Centre in Georgia is listed among the completed works of Massimiliano Fuksas.
facts.quote: Tbilisi Service Centre, Tbilisi, Georgia

facts.fact: The Kuwait Water Towers are a group of 31 water towers in Kuwait City, completed in 1976.
facts.quote: The Kuwait Water Towers are a prominent group of 31 water towers in Kuwait City, Kuwait that were completed in 1976.

facts.fact: In 1965 Kuwait's government asked the Swedish engineering firm VBB to plan and build a modern water-supply system for Kuwait City.
facts.quote: In 1965, the government of Kuwait commissioned the Swedish engineering company of VBB (since 1997 Sweco) to develop and implement a plan for a modern water-supply system for Kuwait City.

facts.fact: VBB built five groups of towers, 31 in all, designed by its chief architect Sune Lindström and known as "the mushroom towers".
facts.quote: The company built five groups of water towers, 31 in total, designed by its chief architect Sune Lindström, called "the mushroom towers".

facts.fact: They are made of standard reinforced concrete, and each holds 3,000 m³ of water.
facts.quote: They were built by VBB out of standard reinforced concrete. Each tower holds 3,000 cubic meters of water.

facts.fact: Each group differs in number, height, colour and ornament, so the towers act as landmarks for their districts.
facts.quote: The tower groups are distinguished by number, height, color and ornamentation and they serve as landmarks for their districts.

facts.fact: For a sixth site the Emir wanted something more spectacular, which became the three Kuwait Towers.
facts.quote: For a sixth site, the Amir of Kuwait, Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmed, wanted a more spectacular design. This last group, known as Kuwait Towers, consists of three towers, two of which also serve as water towers.

facts.fact: The water towers, together with the Kuwait Towers, received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1980.
facts.quote: "The Water Towers" (The Kuwait Tower and the Kuwait Water Towers) were awarded the Aga Khan Award for Architecture (1980 Cycle).

facts.fact: The original White Mosque in Visoko was built in 1477; it was completely rebuilt to a design by Zlatko Ugljen and finished in 1980.
facts.quote: The original mosque was built in 1477, and it was completely reconstructed and finished in 1980 under architect Zlatko Ugljen.

facts.fact: It received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1983, the jury praising its boldness, creativity, originality and innovation.
facts.quote: In 1983 it received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture. The jury commended the mosque for its boldness, creativity and brilliance, as well as its originality and innovation.

facts.fact: Ugljen kept the traditional Bosnian layout of a courtyard leading to a square prayer space under a cupola.
facts.quote: Ugljen used the traditional layout of Bosnian mosques which consist of a courtyard leading to a square praying area, over which rises a cupola.

facts.fact: The plan follows the Bosnian archetype, but the roof is a freely deformed quarter of a cupola pierced by five skylights.
facts.quote: The archetypal Bosnian mosque has a simple square plan crowned by a cupola and entered by means of a small porch. The White Mosque's plan conforms to the archetype, but its roof is a freely deformed quarter of a cupola, pierced by five skylights

facts.fact: Windows of five panels stand for the Five Pillars of Islam and bring light into the interior.
facts.quote: Windows with five panels symbolizes Five Pillars of Islam, but also casts light in the interior.

facts.fact: Walls and cupola are plastered concrete, with pine and white mortar inside, local travertine paving outside and iron-tube minarets.
facts.quote: Building materials used were plastered concrete for walls and cupola, white mortar for the inner walls, a combination of pine wood and white mortar for surfaces of many interior elements, local travertine tiles for exterior paths and courtyard paving, and iron tubes for minarets, while the floors inside of the mosque are covered with green carpet.

facts.fact: Inside and out the mosque is painted white, with a beige floor and green for a few metal elements.
facts.quote: Both the interior and exterior of the mosque are painted white, while the beige color was used for the floor, and green for a few metallic elements, like frames and tubes.

facts.fact: In 2007 Hungarian architects named it one of the three best-designed places of worship in Europe.
facts.quote: In 2007 Hungarian architects called it one of the three best designed places of worship in Europe.

facts.fact: Universiti Teknologi PETRONAS is a private research university founded in 1997 and wholly owned by PETRONAS, Malaysia's oil and gas company.
facts.quote: Universiti Teknologi PETRONAS (UTP) is a private Malaysian Research university established on 10 January 1997. It is wholly owned by Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS), Malaysia's oil and gas multinational corporation.

facts.fact: The campus covers 400 hectares in the new township of Seri Iskandar, Perak.
facts.quote: The campus is built on 400 hectares (990 acres) in the new township of Seri Iskandar, Perak, Malaysia.

facts.fact: The academic complex was designed by Foster and Partners; the first phase was finished in 2004, and the design won an Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2007.
facts.quote: The new academic complex was designed by Foster and Partners, and the first-phase construction was completed in 2004. The design received an Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2007.

facts.fact: The complex is laid out as a five-pointed star made of five semicircles.
facts.quote: The overall layout of the new academic complex is in the shape of a five-pointed star made up by five semicircles.

facts.fact: A "star concept" diagram combining vision, site, programme and quality was used to zone the facilities and start the design.
facts.quote: A 'star concept' diagram, overlaying vision, site, programme and quality, was used as a template to zone various facilities and initiate the preliminary design.

facts.fact: Master planning was finished in 2002 and construction in August 2004.
facts.quote: The process of master planning was completed in 2002 and the construction of the area under consideration was completed in August 2004.

facts.fact: Solar panels with a capacity of 7.3 MWp have been installed on the building roofs.
facts.quote: A total amount of 7.3MWp solar panel were installed at its building rooftop.

facts.fact: A dedicated archaeological museum for Madinat al-Zahra, on the edge of the site, opened in 2009.
facts.quote: A dedicated archeological museum, located on the edge of the site, was opened in 2009.

facts.fact: The Madinat al-Zahra Museum is one of Nieto Sobejano Arquitectos' major works, one of their two projects in Córdoba.
facts.quote: Major works include two projects at Córdoba (the Madinat al-Zahra Museum and the Contemporary Art Centre), the Kunstmuseum Moritzburg Halle (Saale) and extensions to the San Telmo Museum in San Sebastian, and the Joanneum in Graz.

facts.fact: The museum won the European Museum of the Year Award in 2012.
facts.quote: European Museum of the Year Award, Museum es:Museo de Medina Azahara, 2012

facts.fact: The site the museum serves, the Caliphate City of Medina Azahara, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 1 July 2018.
facts.quote: On July 1, 2018, the site was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site with the inscription name "Caliphate City of Medina Azahara".

facts.fact: Majara Residence is a seaside holiday complex on Hormuz Island in the Persian Gulf, in southern Iran; "majara" means "adventure" in Persian.
facts.quote: Majara Residence (Persian: ماجرا, lit. 'Adventure') is a seaside vacation complex on Hormuz Island in the Persian Gulf, south of Iran.

facts.fact: Completed in 2020 and designed by the Tehran firm ZAV Architects, it is the island's first eco-tourism hotel and won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2025.
facts.quote: Completed in 2020, it is the first eco-tourism hotel on the island. It was designed by the Tehran-based architectural firm ZAV Architects and has been recognized internationally, winning several awards, including the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2025.

facts.fact: It is made of 200 domes of different sizes and shapes, some joined together, grouped like a small village 5 km outside the town of Hormuz.
facts.quote: Majara residence consists of 200 domes, some of them interconnected, of different sizes and shapes, organized like a small neighborhood or a village 5 kilometers outside the city of Hormuz.

facts.fact: 130 of the domes hold 17 suites for up to 85 guests; the rest hold galleries, restaurants, cafés, a prayer room, a shop and tourist information.
facts.quote: 130 domes host 17 suites with a maximum capacity of 85 guests. The rest are galleries, restaurants, cafes, a prayer room, a souvenir shop, and tourist info points.

facts.fact: The domes are built with Superadobe: bags filled with on-site earth and sand are layered to form compression structures such as domes.
facts.quote: The technique involves layering bags filled with earth and sand, using on-site soil to create a compression structure like domes and other structural forms.

facts.fact: ZAV adapted the technique to make wider, lower domes, and trained 50 unskilled local workers as master builders.
facts.quote: For Majara, ZAV customized the Superadobe process to allow the creation of larger-radius and lower-height domes. In this process, 50 local unskilled workers were trained to become construction masters.

facts.fact: The earth structure suits the island's arid climate because earth has high thermal mass.
facts.quote: This type of structure is well-suited to the arid climate of the island as earth provides a high thermal mass.

facts.fact: The domes are tinted yellow, red, blue and green; the island's natural coloured ochre was not used, for environmental reasons.
facts.quote: The domes of Majara are colored with tints of yellow, red, blue, and green, and the use of the naturally colored ochre of the island was avoided due to environmental reasons.

facts.fact: The Central Market in Koudougou, Burkina Faso, is among the recipients of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture, in the same cycle as Foster's Universiti Teknologi Petronas.
facts.quote: The award recipients were: Samir Kassir Square, Beirut, Lebanon Rehabilitation of the City of Shibam, Yemen Central Market, Koudougou, Burkina Faso University of Technology Petronas, Bandar Seri Iskandar, Malaysia, by Foster + Partners

facts.fact: Jahad Metro Plaza in Tehran, by KA Architecture Studio, was one of the winners of the 2025 Aga Khan Award for Architecture.
facts.quote: The winners were announced on 2 September 2025: Khudi Bari, in various locations in Bangladesh, by Marina Tabassum Architects West Wusutu Village Community Centre, in Hohhot, China, by Inner Mongolian Grand Architecture Design Co. Ltd / Zhang Pengju Revitalisation of Historic Esna in Egypt, by Takween Integrated Community Development Majara Residence and Community Redevelopment, in Hormuz Island, Iran by ZAV Architects Jahad Metro Plaza, in Tehran, Iran by KA Architecture Studio

facts.fact: The campus of the Entrepreneurship Development Institute in Ahmedabad was one of Bimal Patel's first building designs and won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1992.
facts.quote: In 1990, Patel joined his father's practice in Ahmedabad. One of his first building design projects, a campus for The Entrepreneurship Development Institute, Ahmedabad, won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1992.

facts.fact: Patel's list of works dates the Entrepreneurship Development Institute of India to 1985.
facts.quote: The Entrepreneurship Development Institute of India, Ahmedabad, 1985

facts.fact: The Price Tower is a 19-storey, 67 m skyscraper in Bartlesville, Oklahoma, one of the few high-rises by Frank Lloyd Wright, derived from his 1929 design for apartment towers in New York.
facts.quote: The Price Tower is a nineteen-story, 221-foot-high (67 m) skyscraper at 510 South Dewey Avenue in Bartlesville, Oklahoma, United States. One of the few high-rises designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, the Price Tower is derived from a 1929 proposal for a group of apartment buildings in New York City.

facts.fact: The H. C. Price Company wanted a modern headquarters in Bartlesville, and Harold Price hired Wright to design it in 1952.
facts.quote: The H. C. Price Company wanted to develop a modern headquarters in Bartlesville, and Harold Price hired Wright to design it in 1952.

facts.fact: Wright thought the small-town site ideal, believing skyscrapers belonged in rural areas where they would stand out from the landscape.
facts.quote: Wright thought the Bartlesville location was ideal because he believed that skyscrapers belonged in rural areas, where they stood out from the surrounding landscape.

facts.fact: The plan is set on a grid of parallelograms and 30-60-90 triangles around a pinwheel-shaped core with four piers.
facts.quote: The floor plan is laid out on a grid of parallelograms with 30-60-90 triangles, arranged around a pinwheel-shaped structural core with four piers.

facts.fact: The reinforced-concrete floors cantilever out from the core, and the facade has embossed copper spandrels and louvres, tinted glass and poured stucco.
facts.quote: The facade includes embossed copper spandrels and louvers, tinted glass windows, and poured stucco surfaces. The reinforced-concrete floors are cantilevered outward from the structural core.

facts.fact: It had about 3,900 m² of rentable space, divided into one residential and three office quadrants.
facts.quote: As built, the Price Tower had about 42,000 square feet (3,900 m2) of rentable space, split across one residential and three office quadrants.

facts.fact: It was among the first skyscrapers designed with both apartments and offices from the start.
facts.quote: The structure was also among the first skyscrapers with both apartments and offices from the outset.

facts.fact: It received the AIA Twenty-five Year Award in 1983 and is a National Historic Landmark.
facts.quote: It received the American Institute of Architects' Twenty-five Year Award in 1983 and has been designated a National Historic Landmark.

facts.fact: The Sainsbury Wing, a 1991 extension to the west of the National Gallery in London by Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown, is a significant example of Postmodernist architecture in Britain.
facts.quote: The Sainsbury Wing, a 1991 extension to the west by Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown, is a significant example of Postmodernist architecture in Britain.

facts.fact: A donation made in April 1985 by Lord Sainsbury of Preston Candover and his brothers Simon and Sir Timothy Sainsbury paid for its construction.
facts.quote: In April 1985 Lord Sainsbury of Preston Candover and his brothers, Simon Sainsbury and Sir Timothy Sainsbury, had made a donation that would enable the construction of the Sainsbury Wing.

facts.fact: A £375 million expansion announced in 2025 includes a new wing behind the Sainsbury Wing.
facts.quote: In September 2025, the National Gallery announced plans for a £375 million expansion project, provisionally titled 'Project Domani'. The initiative includes the construction of a new wing behind the existing Sainsbury Wing and a policy change allowing the acquisition of works created after 1900.

facts.fact: Monterey Bay Aquarium, a nonprofit public aquarium in Monterey, California, focuses on the habitats of Monterey Bay and was the first to show a living kelp forest when it opened in October 1984.
facts.quote: Monterey Bay Aquarium is a nonprofit public aquarium in Monterey, California, United States. Known for its regional focus on the marine habitats of Monterey Bay, it was the first to exhibit a living kelp forest when it opened in October 1984.

facts.fact: It was built on the site of a defunct sardine cannery and has been recognised by the American Institute of Architects for its architecture.
facts.quote: Monterey Bay Aquarium was built at the site of a defunct sardine cannery and has been recognized for its architectural achievements by the American Institute of Architects.

facts.fact: The architects, EHDD, chose to rebuild the Hovden Cannery rather than demolish it, saying demolition would be "a big disservice" to visitors and the community.
facts.quote: Those involved intended to reconstruct Hovden Cannery rather than destroy it, and EHDD acknowledged that the latter would be "a big disservice to our visiting public and to the community".

facts.fact: Concrete parts of the cannery were kept: its warehouse became offices, a seawater system replaced its pump house, and the building was built around its boiler house, kept as a non-working exhibit.
facts.quote: Concrete sections of the building were able to be kept, but other areas were repurposed; the cannery's old warehouse was converted into administrative offices, and a seawater system for the aquatic exhibits replaced the cannery's pump house that brought fish to the warehouse from floating storage tanks in the bay. The facility was constructed around the cannery's boiler house, which is preserved as a non-functioning public exhibit.

facts.fact: Nearly half of the aquarium stands over the bay in water up to 37 m deep, so foundations had to be built at low tide, often at night.
facts.quote: Nearly half of the aquarium would be located over the bay in depths of up to 120 ft (37 m), requiring foundational elements to be installed during low tide, which often occurred at night.

facts.fact: The building echoes the cannery in its windows, plain cement walls, protection from waves and storms and many roofs, with exposed pipes and ducts in the industrial style of Cannery Row.
facts.quote: Various elements of the building mirrored that of Hovden Cannery, including its windows (to let in sunlight), plain cement walls, structural protection from waves and storms, and its many roofs. Exposed pipes and ducts along the ceiling also contributed to the industrial style of buildings on Cannery Row.

facts.fact: When it opened on 20 October 1984 it was the largest public aquarium in the United States.
facts.quote: When Monterey Bay Aquarium opened on October 20, 1984, it was the largest public aquarium in the United States.

facts.fact: EHDD won an AIA National Honor Award for the design in 1988, and the building received the AIA's national Twenty-five Year Award in 2016.
facts.quote: For its design, EHDD was awarded a National Honor Award from the American Institute of Architects in 1988. The institute's state chapter in California gave the facility its Twenty-five Year Award in 2011 and, in 2016, it was awarded the national Twenty-five Year Award, described as "a benchmark and role model for aquariums everywhere."

facts.fact: Eric Owen Moss's list of works places The Box in Culver City, California, in 1994.
facts.quote: The Box, Culver City, California, US, 1994

facts.fact: In 2020 Moss's Conjunctive Points – The New City in Culver City received the AIA Twenty-five Year Award, given to buildings that have stood the test of time for 25–35 years.
facts.quote: In 2020 Conjunctive Points – The New City was awarded the AIA Twenty-five Year Award. The award is conferred on a building that has stood the test of time for 25–35 years and continues to set standards of excellence for its architectural design and significance.

facts.fact: A 1996 book from Princeton Architectural Press, edited by Preston Scott Cohen and Brooke Hodge, is devoted to The Box.
facts.quote: Preston Scott Cohen, Brooke Hodge (eds.), Eric Owen Moss. The Box, Princeton Architectural Press, New York 1996.

facts.fact: The Washington Metro's first stretch opened on 27 March 1976: five Red Line stations from Rhode Island Avenue to Farragut North.
facts.quote: The first portion of the system opened on March 27, 1976, with 4.6 miles (7.4 km) available on the Red Line with five stations from Rhode Island Avenue to Farragut North, all in Washington, D.C.

facts.fact: Harry Weese designed the first group of stations on the Washington Metro.
facts.quote: Weese is best known as the designer and architect of the first group of stations in the Washington Metro system.

facts.fact: The underground stations were built as cathedral-like concrete arches lit by soft, indirect light.
facts.quote: Underground stations were built with cathedral-like arches of concrete, highlighted by soft, indirect lighting.

facts.fact: Critic Herbert Muschamp wrote that the vaulted ceilings where lines cross induce an almost religious sense of awe.
facts.quote: Muschamp noted that the vaulted ceilings at the crossings of subway lines "induce an almost religious sense of awe".

facts.fact: In 2014 the AIA gave the system its Twenty-five Year Award, citing Weese's common design kit of parts, which still guides new stations.
facts.quote: In January 2014, the AIA announced that it would present its Twenty-five Year Award to the Washington Metro system for "an architectural design of enduring significance" that "has stood the test of time by embodying architectural excellence for 25 to 35 years". The announcement cited the key role of Harry Weese, who conceived and implemented a "common design kit-of-parts" which continues to guide the construction of new Metro stations over a quarter-century later.

facts.fact: In a 2007 public poll for the AIA, the vaulted stations were the only brutalist design among America's 150 favourite buildings.
facts.quote: In 2007, the design of the Washington Metro's vaulted-ceiling stations was voted number 106 on the "America's Favorite Architecture" list compiled by the American Institute of Architects (AIA), and was the only brutalist design to win a place among the 150 selected by this public survey.

facts.fact: Massimo Vignelli suggested the name Metro and designed the system's signage.
facts.quote: The name Metro was suggested by Massimo Vignelli, who designed the signage for the system as well as for the New York City Subway.

facts.fact: The Florey Building is a modernist student residence in Oxford by James Stirling, the last of his listed 'Red Trilogy' with the Leicester Engineering and Cambridge History Faculty buildings.
facts.quote: The Florey Building is a modernist student accommodation building by James Stirling in Oxford, United Kingdom. It is the third and last building of “The Red Trilogy” (together with the Leicester Engineering Faculty building and the Cambridge History Faculty building), all of which are now listed.

facts.fact: It was built from 1968 to 1971 and, like the rest of the trilogy, uses red industrial bricks and tiles with standard factory-made glazing.
facts.quote: Construction took place between 1968 and 1971. The completion date was almost a year and a half later than promised due to a delay of the construction drawings to the contractors on site. The building was the third in Stirling's "Red Trilogy", and follows the earlier two in employing the same traditional red industrial bricks and tiles and non-bespoke factory-made glazing systems, as well as sculptural and unusual forms in the overall design.

facts.fact: The structure is 11 irregular A-shaped reinforced concrete frames, 7 m apart, linked by spine beams and clad in red ceramic tiles.
facts.quote: The main structure consists of 11 reinforced concrete frames of irregular A shape placed at 7 m spacings linked by spine beams at each floor. Red ceramic tiles clad the main structure and paving for the courtyard.

facts.fact: The plan is a horseshoe open to the north; every room has floor-to-ceiling glass facing the court and a view across the River Cherwell.
facts.quote: The building is set back from the road and designed in a horse shoe shape, with the open side facing north. All residential rooms feature floor-to-ceiling glazing, facing the inner court of the building. Only a few small windows face outward and are visible from the outside. This gives every room a view across the River Cherwell to the Angel and Greyhound Meadow beyond.

facts.fact: It holds 74 single rooms on four levels, with double-height gallery rooms for graduates on top.
facts.quote: There are 74 single rooms split over four levels, with a top level of double-height gallery rooms for graduates and one apartment for a Bachelor fellow.

facts.fact: It was commissioned for The Queen's College by its Provost Howard Florey, the penicillin Nobel laureate, and named after him.
facts.quote: The building was commissioned for The Queen's College by the then Provost of the college, Sir Howard Florey—later Lord Florey of Adelaide—who shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine for synthesising the drug penicillin for use, saving hundreds of thousands of lives in the aftermath of WWII. The Florey Building was named after the Provost, following his death during the week that building work commenced on site, in 1968.

facts.fact: Listed Grade II in 2009, it was upgraded to Grade II* in December 2018.
facts.quote: A decade later, the Florey Building was listed at Grade II in 2009. An application for it to be upgraded, made by the C20 Society, was resisted by The Queen's College, who employed consultants to argue that the lower Grade II was appropriate. However, the building was re-designated at Grade II* in December 2018.

facts.fact: Empty since 2018–19, the college said in 2024 it would mothball the building for the foreseeable future.
facts.quote: The building freehold is still owned by The Queen's College, but since the academic year 2018–19 the Florey Building lay unoccupied and boarded up. The college announced in 2024 that it had decided to 'mothball the Florey Building for the foreseeable future'.

facts.fact: Siza's Church of Santa Maria in Marco de Canaveses is dated 1990–1996 in the list of his works.
facts.quote: 1990-1996: Church of Santa Maria, Marco de Canaveses, Portugal.

facts.fact: The Zénith music hall in Strasbourg is listed among Massimiliano Fuksas's main works.
facts.quote: Zénith Music Hall, Strasbourg, France

facts.fact: Fuksas has worked in partnership with his wife Doriana Mandrelli since 1985.
facts.quote: From 1985 he has worked in partnership with his second wife, Doriana Mandrelli, who graduated in architecture in Paris in 2007.

facts.fact: Camp de Rivesaltes (Camp Joffre) was a Second World War internment and transit camp in southern France.
facts.quote: The Camp de Rivesaltes, also known as Camp Joffre, was an internment and transit camp in the commune of Rivesaltes in the department of Pyrénées-Orientales of the French Southern Zone during World War Two.

facts.fact: In 1942, 2,313 foreign Jews, 209 of them children, were sent from Rivesaltes via Drancy to Auschwitz and murdered.
facts.quote: Between August 11 and October 20, 1942, 2,313 foreign Jews, including 209 children were transferred from Rivesaltes via the Drancy internment camp to the Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz, where they were murdered.

facts.fact: The military camp itself was built in 1938, a few miles from Perpignan.
facts.quote: The military camp was built in 1938, a few miles from Perpignan.

facts.fact: A 1997 petition signed by Simone Veil and over a thousand others opposed the camp's threatened demolition.
facts.quote: In 1997, following the discovery of part of the camp's archives in a rubbish dump, a collective petition "To the living memory of the camp of Rivesaltes" (Pour la mémoire vivante du camp de Rivesaltes) was signed by Simone Veil, Claude Simon, Edgar Morin and over a thousand other citizens, to protest against the camp's threatened destruction.

facts.fact: In 2000 the site was added to France's supplementary list of historic monuments.
facts.quote: In 2000, the French Ministry of Culture included the site in its supplementary list of monuments historiques, and part of the land was purchased from the French government by the General Council of the Pyrénées-Orientales.

facts.fact: Rudy Ricciotti won the architecture competition for the memorial in January 2006.
facts.quote: In January 2006, Rudy Ricciotti won an architecture competition for the memorial project, which Robert Badinter agreed to sponsor.

facts.fact: Prime Minister Manuel Valls inaugurated the memorial site on 16 October 2015.
facts.quote: On 16 October 2015, the site was inaugurated by French Prime Minister Manuel Valls.

facts.fact: The last residents left the camp in February 1977.
facts.quote: The last residents left the camp in February 1977.

facts.fact: The Katyń Museum in Warsaw shows objects, documents and personal effects from the site of the Katyn massacre.
facts.quote: Objects, documents and personal effects from the site of the Katyn massacre can be seen in the museum.

facts.fact: The museum was nominated for the EU Prize for Contemporary Architecture in 2017.
facts.quote: In 2017 museum was nominated for European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture award.

facts.fact: The museum institution was established in 1993.
facts.quote: The museum was established in 1993.

facts.fact: The Saw Swee Hock Student Centre, LSE's first new campus building in over 40 years, opened in January 2014 after a RIBA-run design competition.
facts.quote: The first new campus building for more than 40 years, the Saw Swee Hock Student Centre, named after the Singaporean statistician and philanthropist, opened in January 2014 following an architectural design competition managed by RIBA Competitions.

facts.fact: It houses the Students' Union, accommodation and careers offices, a bar, events space, gym, rooftop terrace, café, dance studio and media centre.
facts.quote: The building provides accommodation for the LSE Students' Union, LSE accommodation office and LSE careers service as well as a bar, events space, gymnasium, rooftop terrace, learning café, dance studio, and media centre.

facts.fact: Designed by O'Donnell & Tuomey, it was rated BREEAM 'Outstanding', won a RIBA National Award and was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize.
facts.quote: Designed by architectural practice O'Donnell & Tuomey, the building achieved a BREEAM 'Outstanding' rating for environmental sustainability, won multiple awards including the RIBA National Award and London Building of the Year Award, and was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize.
