facts.fact: The practice lists the project as running from 2009 to 2015.
facts.quote: LSE Saw Swee Hock Student Centre, London, UK, 2009–2015.

facts.fact: O'Donnell + Tuomey won the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 2015.
facts.quote: In 2015, O'Donnell + Tuomey won the 2015 RIBA Royal Gold Medal, the world's most prestigious architecture award.

facts.fact: The Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision is an archive centre and museum in Hilversum.
facts.quote: The Dutch Institute for Sound and Vision (Dutch: Nederlands Instituut voor Beeld en Geluid, NIBG), founded as Dutch Audiovisual Archive (Dutch: Nederlands Audiovisueel Archief, NAA) is an archive centre and museum located in Hilversum, Netherlands.

facts.fact: It is the business archive of Dutch public broadcasting as well as a heritage institute open to researchers and the public.
facts.quote: It is the business archive of the Dutch public broadcasting system as well as a cultural heritage institute for researchers and the public.

facts.fact: As of 2014 it held more than 750,000 hours of material dating back to 1898.
facts.quote: As of 2014, the institute has more than 750,000 hours of material dating back to 1898, making it one of the largest audiovisual archives in Europe.

facts.fact: Koen van Velsen is known for the Groot Klimmendaal rehabilitation centre, among other works.
facts.quote: Koen Jozef van Velsen (born 17 July 1952) is an architect from Hilversum, Netherlands known for his design work on the Discothèque Slinger, rehabilitation center Groot Klimmendaal and the library in Zeewolde.

facts.fact: Van Velsen's work follows a contextual design approach rather than a personal aesthetic.
facts.quote: His work employs a contextual design approach, free of a personal esthetic.

facts.fact: Wiel Arets's Hedge House in Wijlre dates from 1998–2001.
facts.quote: Hedge House (Wijlre, 1998–2001)

facts.fact: Peckham Library is a library and community building in south-east London, designed by Alsop and Störmer and engineered by AKT II.
facts.quote: Peckham Library is a library and community building situated in Peckham in south-east London, United Kingdom. It was designed by Alsop and Störmer, engineered by AKT II and won the Stirling Prize for Architecture in 2000.

facts.fact: It is shaped like an upside-down L, its upper part held on thin steel pillars at seemingly random angles, and clad in pre-patinated copper.
facts.quote: The building is shaped like an inverted capital letter 'L', with the upper part supported by thin steel pillars set at apparently random angles. The exterior is clad with pre-patinated copper.

facts.fact: Alsop lifted a conventional library footprint into the air, making a public space underneath and taking the reading room away from street noise.
facts.quote: Alsop has taken the plan footprint of a conventional library and elevated it to create a public space beneath the building and to remove the quiet reading space from street level noise.

facts.fact: It has five floors, with the library itself on the fourth floor.
facts.quote: The building has five floors in total, with the library service taking up the fourth floor.

facts.fact: It opened on 8 March 2000.
facts.quote: The library opened to the public on 8 March 2000, with an official opening by Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport, Chris Smith, on 15 May 2000.

facts.fact: It won the 2000 Stirling Prize, the UK's most prestigious architecture award.
facts.quote: In 2000, Alsop won the Stirling Prize, the most prestigious architecture award in the United Kingdom, for the Peckham Library in London.

facts.fact: It draws over half a million visitors a year.
facts.quote: The building attracts over half a million visitors per year.

facts.fact: Newport Street Gallery was created by artist Damien Hirst to show his own art collection and host exhibitions that interest him.
facts.quote: The Newport Street Gallery is an art gallery in London, England, created by contemporary artist Damien Hirst for the display of works from his personal art collection, and as a venue to put on exhibitions of interest to him.

facts.fact: It opened in October 2015 and includes a café, shop and offices for Hirst's company.
facts.quote: Hirst announced plans for the gallery in March 2012, with a stated intent of realising "Hirst's long-term ambition to share his art collection with the public", opening in October 2015. It includes a cafe, gallery shop and offices for Hirst's company.

facts.fact: The core is a Grade II listed 1913 workshop for theatre carpentry and scenery, designed by the district surveyor John Woodward.
facts.quote: The building is a former theatre carpentry and scenery production workshop, dating from 1913. It was designed by John Woodward, the London County Council's district surveyor for the area. It is Grade II listed.

facts.fact: Caruso St John redesigned it as a gallery, and it won the RIBA Stirling Prize in October 2016.
facts.quote: For its conversion to the gallery, the building was redesigned by Caruso St John. The design was praised for its "virtuosity", and in October 2016 it won the RIBA Stirling Prize.

facts.fact: It covers 3,400 m² with six exhibition spaces on two levels, one 11 m high.
facts.quote: The gallery spans 37,000 square feet (3,400 m2) and includes six exhibition spaces – one with a ceiling height of 11 metres (36 ft) – split over two levels.

facts.fact: The Everyman stands at the north end of Hope Street in Liverpool; it was founded in 1964 and completely rebuilt between 2011 and 2014.
facts.quote: The Everyman Theatre stands at the north end of Hope Street in Liverpool, Merseyside, England.  It was founded in 1964, in Hope Hall (once a chapel, then a cinema), in an area of Liverpool noted for its bohemian environment and political edge, and quickly built a reputation for ground-breaking work. The Everyman was completely rebuilt between 2011 and 2014.

facts.fact: The original building was Hope Hall, a dissenters' chapel of 1837.
facts.quote: The building was constructed as Hope Hall, a dissenters' chapel built in 1837.

facts.fact: The old theatre closed in July 2011 to be completely rebuilt.
facts.quote: In July 2011 the theatre closed to be completely rebuilt.

facts.fact: The new Everyman reopened in February 2014 and won Haworth Tompkins the RIBA Stirling Prize that October.
facts.quote: The Everyman reopened in February 2014. In October 2014, the Stirling Prize from the Royal Institute of British Architects for the best British building of the year was awarded to Haworth Tompkins for their work on the new Everyman.

facts.fact: Haworth Tompkins is a London studio focusing on theatres and cultural buildings.
facts.quote: Based in London, the studio works throughout the public, private and subsidised sectors at a wide spectrum, focusing on theatrical and culturally oriented buildings, and even schools, galleries, housing, offices, shops and factories.

facts.fact: The Velodrom is an indoor cycling arena in Prenzlauer Berg, Berlin, holding up to 12,000 people.
facts.quote: The Velodrom (velodrome) is an indoor track cycling arena, in the Prenzlauer Berg locality of Berlin, Germany. Holding up to 12,000 people, it was also Berlin's largest concert venue, until the opening of Uber Arena in 2008.

facts.fact: It and its swimming pool were built for Berlin's unsuccessful bid for the 2000 Olympics.
facts.quote: It is part of a larger complex, which includes a swimming pool as well, built in the course of the unsuccessful Berlin application for the 2000 Summer Olympics.

facts.fact: Dominique Perrault won the international competition in 1992.
facts.quote: The building was designed by French architect Dominique Perrault who won an international design competition in 1992 and was awarded the German Award of Architecture, second prize for the velodrome and the Olympic swimming pool.

facts.fact: The idea was an apple orchard with two buildings, one round and one rectangular, set into the ground and covered in shimmering wire gauze that reads more like water than buildings.
facts.quote: The idea was to create an orchard of apple trees with two buildings set into the ground, one round and the other rectangular, covered with a wire gauze, which shimmer in the sunlight and appear to be stretches of water more than buildings.

facts.fact: Its steel roof, 142 m across, is Europe's largest.
facts.quote: The arena is famous for its steel roof construction – with a diameter of 142 meters, it has Europe's largest steel roof.

facts.fact: It replaced the Werner-Seelenbinder-Halle, demolished in 1993.
facts.quote: It replaced the former Werner-Seelenbinder-Halle, which was demolished in 1993.

facts.fact: Perrault's office dates the velodrome and Olympic pool 1992–1999.
facts.quote: 1992-1999: Olympic Velodrome and Olympic swimming pool, Berlin, Germany

facts.fact: The complex was built in 1995 for the Neurosciences Institute on the Scripps Research Institute campus, designed by Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects.
facts.quote: In 1993, the NSI moved to San Diego, California—first into temporary quarters and then, in 1995, into a newly constructed complex on the campus of The Scripps Research Institute (TSRI). Designed by the firm Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects, the three-building complex received much acclaim for its Modernist style and especially for an auditorium that became a favored venue for music and performing arts in the area.

facts.fact: Founder Gerald Edelman wanted a 'scientific monastery' with few rules and endless chances for scientists to meet.
facts.quote: Edelman has said that, in selecting an architect, his goal was to find one who could realize his vision of a "scientific monastery" where creative study of the brain could be conducted with few constraining rules and unlimited opportunities for communication.

facts.fact: It won an AIA Honor Award for Architecture in 1997; Severud Associates were the structural engineers.
facts.quote: The resulting complex, designed by Tod Williams and Billie Tsien, has been awarded numerous honors, including the Honor Award for Architecture from the American Institute of Architects in 1997.  The structural engineering firm chosen for this project was Severud Associates.

facts.fact: The 352-seat auditorium, made with acoustician Cyril Harris, is lined with faceted plaster panels so the same sound reaches every seat.
facts.quote: Noted acoustician Cyril Harris worked with the architects to create the 352-seat auditorium. Considered to be among the most acoustically impressive small performance halls in the United States, the auditorium was built with an original system of faceted, sound-dispersing plaster panels that cover its walls and ceiling, so that the same sound can be heard in every seat.

facts.fact: The three-building complex stands on Torrey Pines Mesa in San Diego among research institutes and UC San Diego.
facts.quote: Between 1995 and 2012, the NSI occupied a three-building complex located on Torrey Pines Mesa in San Diego. It was bordered by TSRI to the west, the Sanford-Burnham Institute to the north, the University of California, San Diego to the south, and numerous biotechnology and pharmaceutical research companies to the east and in the immediate surrounding area.

facts.fact: After the institute's 2012 financial crisis the buildings passed to the Scripps Research Institute.
facts.quote: Following NSI's 2012 restructuring, the buildings were taken over by TSRI.

facts.fact: Moesgaard Museum is a regional museum of archaeology and ethnography near Aarhus, Denmark.
facts.quote: Moesgaard Museum (MOMU) is a Danish regional museum dedicated to archaeology and ethnography. It is located east of Beder, a village and suburb of Aarhus, Denmark.

facts.fact: Its new building by Henning Larsen Architects, holding exhibitions and academic offices, opened in 2014.
facts.quote: A large new museum building, designed by Henning Larsen Architects, housing both public exhibitions and the headquarters for academic activities, was inaugurated in 2014.

facts.fact: The building is organised around a broad central staircase, with changing world exhibitions above and permanent Danish and European displays below.
facts.quote: The museum building is constructed around a broad central staircase. The upper levels show changing exhibits of history and culture from around the world, while the lower levels house the permanent exhibitions on Danish, Scandinavian, and European history and culture.

facts.fact: Its grass-covered roof was part of the course of the 2019 World Cross Country Championships.
facts.quote: In 2019, the landscape around Moesgaard Museum was used for the IAAF 2019 Cross Country World Championships. The route included the museum buildings grass covered roof.

facts.fact: Its collection includes the Grauballe Man, the world's best-preserved bog body.
facts.quote: The museum's exhibitions present several unrivaled archaeological findings from Denmark's ancient past, among others the Grauballe Man, the world's best preserved bog body, and the large ritual weapon caches from Illerup Ådal, testifying to the power struggles and warfare of the Iron Age.

facts.fact: The museum building received the Chicago Athenaeum's International Architecture Award in 2015.
facts.quote: 2015 The International Architecture Award (The Chicago Athenaeum: Museum of Architecture and Design) for Moesgaard Museum

facts.fact: Goldsmith Street is public housing built to the passive house standard in Norwich, designed by Mikhail Riches and Cathy Hawley.
facts.quote: Goldsmith Street public housing (passive houses) in Norwich, designed by Mikhail Riches and Cathy Hawley.

facts.fact: Magdalene College's New Library, designed by Niall McLaughlin Architects, won the Stirling Prize in October 2022.

facts.fact: The Glucksman is an art museum at University College Cork.

facts.fact: Designed by O'Donnell & Tuomey with Arup, it won a Civic Trust award and a RIBA award and was shortlisted for the 2005 Stirling Prize.

facts.quote: American Institute of Architects, Excellence in Design Award 2003.

facts.fact: It is one of the notable projects of Ted Cullinan's practice.
facts.quote: Notable projects include the Charles Cryer Theatre, Carshalton (completed in 1991), the Fountains Abbey Visitor Centre (completed 1992), the Centre for Mathematical Sciences (Cambridge) (completed 2003), the Weald and Downland Gridshell (2002, nominated for the Stirling Prize) and the new library at Fitzwilliam College, Cambridge (opened 2010).

facts.fact: The Hall of Nations was an exhibition hall at Pragati Maidan, New Delhi, opened in 1972 to mark 25 years of Indian independence.
facts.quote: The Hall of Nations was an iconic exhibition hall inaugurated in 1972 as part of the Pragati Maidan complex in New Delhi, India. It was built to commemorate 25 years of Indian independence.

facts.fact: It was the world's first, and at the time largest-span, space-frame structure in reinforced concrete.
facts.quote: Inaugurated by then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi for the India International Trade Fair called Asia 72, it was the world’s first and, at the time, the largest-span space-frame structure built in reinforced concrete.

facts.fact: It was a group of four halls of different sizes linked by ramps.
facts.quote: The Hall of Nations comprised a group of four halls of varying sizes, interconnected by a system of ramps.

facts.fact: Raj Rewal designed it and Mahendra Raj engineered the structure; it took 22 months to build.
facts.quote: It was designed by the Indian architect Raj Rewal, and structurally engineered by Mahendra Raj. The hall served as a venue for trade fair exhibitions. The construction took 22 months and was subsequently deemed the venue for the 1972 International Trade Fair.

facts.fact: MoMA and the Centre Pompidou protested the 2015 plans to demolish it.
facts.quote: When the demolition of the Hall of Nations as part of the redevelopment plans were revealed in November 2015, it led to protest not merely by local architects but also by museums like the MoMA; the Centre Pompidou in Paris requested the Government of India to consider preserving the complex of buildings as heritage structures.

facts.fact: It was demolished overnight in April 2017 while its heritage status was still before the Delhi High Court; The New York Times called it a brutalist masterpiece.
facts.quote: Legal interventions were still ongoing in the Delhi High Court when the structure was demolished overnight in April 2017. The demolition of the building, which was considered iconic for its architecture, led to widespread national and global disapproval. It was described in The New York Times as a brutalist masterpiece and one of the world's largest-span space frame concrete structures, when built.

facts.fact: The Bharat Mandapam convention centre now stands on its site.
facts.quote: This new complex, named Bharat Mandapam, stands on the site of the former Hall of Nations.

facts.fact: The Shri Ram Centre is one of Delhi's noted theatre venues, at Mandi House on Safdar Hashmi Marg near the National School of Drama.
facts.quote: The Shri Ram Centre for Performing Arts (SRCPA) commonly referred as Shri Ram Centre, is one of Delhi's noted theatre organisation and theatre venues. It is situated at Mandi House on Safdar Hashmi Marg, New Delhi, close to the Shriram Bharatiya Kala Kendra, Kamani Auditorium, Triveni Kala Sangam and the National School of Drama.

facts.fact: The brutalist building was built 1966–1969 to designs by Shiv Nath Prasad and Mahendra Raj, with advice from theatre director Ebrahim Alkazi, and opened in 1971.
facts.quote: The present building of the Centre opened in 1971. The Brutalist building, built between 1966 and 1969, was designed by Shiv Nath Prasad and Mahendra Raj with help from theatre doyen, Ebrahim Alkazi, and was constructed under the overall supervision of industrialist Vinay Bharat Ram of Shriram Group (DCM Ltd.), from the industrialist family of Lala Shri Ram.

facts.fact: Its proscenium auditorium seats 375 on two levels: 300 in the stalls and 75 in the balcony.
facts.quote: The Shankar Lal Murli Dhar Auditorium is a proscenium theatre with a capacity of 375 people at two levels; 300 in the stall & 75 in the balcony.

facts.fact: A basement storage area became the 'Basement Theatre', a venue for experimental work for more than two decades.
facts.quote: He converted a basement storage area into an intimate performance venue, 'Basement Theatre', which soon got associated with experimental theatre and smaller productions. It contributed to the development of alternative theatrical spaces within Delhi's Mandi House cultural district, and remained active for more than two decades.

facts.fact: Shiv Nath Prasad was an Indian architect known for brutalist designs, called the 'Le Corbusier of India'.
facts.quote: Shiv Nath Prasad (1922–c. 2002) was an Indian architect and urban planner known for his Brutalist architecture designs. He was also called the "Le Corbusier of India".

facts.fact: The inaugural play, Sai Paranjpye's Ek Tamasha Achchha Khasa, was staged on 26 February 1971.
facts.quote: Ek Tamasha Achchha Khasa, a Hindi play written and directed by Sai Paranjpye, was the inaugural play at the Centre, staged on 26 February 1971, in which G. P. Deshpande played the lead role of a simpleton king.

facts.fact: The India International Centre is a non-official meeting place for cultural and intellectual life in New Delhi.
facts.quote: It serves as a meeting place for cultural and intellectual offerings; while maintaining its non-official character, non-aligned motivations and remains uncommitted to any particular form of governmental, political, economic or religious affiliation.

facts.fact: Joseph Allen Stein designed the main complex and its annex beside Lodhi Gardens; his many buildings nearby gave the area the nickname 'Steinabad'.
facts.quote: The centre's main complex and its annex (located adjacent to Lodhi Gardens) were designed by the architect Joseph Allen Stein. There are several other major institutions around the centre, which are also designed by Stein, giving the area the popular name of 'Steinabad'.

facts.fact: Prince Akihito of Japan laid the foundation stone in 1960, and President S. Radhakrishnan opened it in 1962.
facts.quote: The centre's foundation stone was laid in 1960 by Japanese Prince Akihito, who had come to India for his honeymoon; it was inaugurated in 1962 by S. Radhakrishnan, the 2nd President of India.

facts.fact: The centre calls itself 'Triveni', a structure of three, for its intellectual, cultural and social streams.
facts.quote: According to its official blurb, the centre is alluded to as 'Triveni', which in Sanskrit means 'a structure of three', as it provides three main activity streams:

facts.fact: The annex was opened in 1996.
facts.quote: The centre's annex was inaugurated in 1996 by Karan Singh, the president of IIC.

facts.fact: Its Gandhi-King Plaza was opened by Indira Gandhi on 21 January 1970.
facts.quote: The centre's Gandhi-King Plaza, named after Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr., was inaugurated on 21 January 1970 by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

facts.fact: Masjid-e-Tooba, known as Gol Masjid (Round Mosque), stands in Phase II of the Defence Housing Authority, Karachi.
facts.quote: Masjid-e-Tooba (Urdu: مسجد طوبٰی) also known as Gol Masjid (lit. 'Round Mosque'), is a mosque located in the city of Karachi in Sindh province of Pakistan. It is situated near the main Korangi Road in Phase II of the Defence Housing Authority, Karachi.

facts.fact: Building began in 1966 and was completed in 1969.
facts.quote: The construction of the mosque began in 1966. It took three years and was completed in 1969.

facts.fact: It was designed by architect Babar Hameed Chauhan with structural engineer Zaheer Haider Naqvi.
facts.quote: The mosque was designed by Pakistani architect Babar Hameed Chauhan and the structural engineer for the project was Zaheer Haider Naqvi.

facts.fact: It holds up to 5,000 people in a prayer hall with no pillars or columns under a 65 m dome.
facts.quote: The mosque has the capacity to hold up to 5,000 people. It has praying hall under wider dome without any pillar or column. The dome has the diameter of 212 feet (65 m).

facts.fact: It has a single minaret 37 m tall.
facts.quote: It has single minaret with a height of 120 feet (37 m).

facts.fact: It is considered the world's largest single-dome mosque without pillars in its prayer hall; the dome rests on a low surrounding wall.
facts.quote: The mosque is considered to be the largest single-dome mosque in the world with no pillars in its central prayer hall. Its huge dome is supported on a low surrounding wall.

facts.fact: The Teacher-Student Centre (TSC) is a building on the University of Dhaka campus in Shahbagh, established in 1961.
facts.quote: Teacher-Student Centre (Bengali: শিক্ষক-ছাত্র কেন্দ্র, romanized: Sikkhok-Chhatra Kendra), also known as TSC, is a building on the Dhaka University campus in Shahbagh, Dhaka, Bangladesh. The centre was established in 1961 by the Dhaka University by the Division of Public Affairs.

facts.fact: It was paid for by the Pakistan Government and the Ford Foundation.
facts.quote: The construction of the Teacher-Student Centre was financed by the Pakistan Government and the Ford foundation.

facts.fact: Doxiadis's list of works dates the TSC to 1961.
facts.quote: Teacher-Student Centre (TSC), University of Dhaka, Bangladesh; 1961

facts.fact: Arranged around a court, it has a second 'butterfly' roof over the front of the main block that helps keep it cool.
facts.quote: Arranged around a court, it has an extra butterfly canopy (double roof) extended over the main block at the front, which helps to keep the Centre cool.

facts.fact: With dining, meeting, library, art and music rooms, stages and halls, it is the social and cultural heart of the campus.
facts.quote: The complex contains dining rooms, meeting rooms, libraries, art and music rooms, stages, a multipurpose hall, game rooms, a film lab, rehearsal rooms, and more. As a result, the Teacher-Student Centre forms the social and cultural heart of the campus.

facts.fact: Extensions built in the 1980s allow north–south cross-ventilation.
facts.quote: The complex has some extensions which were built during the 1980s that allowed north–south cross-ventilation.

facts.fact: Many important political meetings were held there during the Bangladesh Liberation War.
facts.quote: Many historically important political meetings and discussions were held at the Teacher-Student Centre during the Bangladesh Liberation War.

facts.fact: Kunlé Adeyemi of NLÉ proposed the floating school in 2013 as a prototype that floats with the Makoko waterfront community instead of flooding on land.
facts.quote: In 2013, a Nigerian architect, Kunlé Adeyemi of NLÉ proposed to transform the water slum status of the Makoko waterfront community to a floating island by creating a functional building prototype. This prototype would have the ability to combat previous issues with flooding on land by having the school float alongside the community.

facts.fact: It was built from local materials such as bamboo and timber, with wood used for structure, support and finishes.
facts.quote: The floating school utilized local materials such as bamboo, timber and resources to produce architecture that applied to the physical, social needs of people and reflects the culture of the community. Wood was the major material for the structure, support and finishing of school building.

facts.fact: The building had a triangular A-frame section, with classrooms on the second tier behind adjustable louvres.
facts.quote: The form of the school building was a triangular A-Frame section with about 1,000-square-foot play area. The classrooms are located on the second tier and are partially enclosed with adjustable louvered slats.

facts.fact: A playground sat below the classrooms and an open-air classroom on the roof.
facts.quote: There is a playground below the classroom while the roof contains an additional open air classroom.

facts.fact: It had solar cells, rainwater collection and composting toilets, and floated on about 250 plastic barrels.
facts.quote: Sustainable features include application of solar cells to the roof, rainwater catchment systems and composting toilets. The structure is also designed to use about 250 plastic barrels to float on the waters and be naturally ventilated and aerated.

facts.fact: The design won the 2013 AR+D award for emerging architecture and was shortlisted for the Design Museum's 2014 Design of the Year.
facts.quote: The floating school design won the 2013 AR+D award for emerging architecture and was shortlisted for the London Design Museum's 2014 Design of the Year award.

facts.fact: It was abandoned in March 2016 over safety concerns and collapsed in a storm in June 2016.
facts.quote: The school was abandoned in March 2016 over safety concerns and collapsed in a storm in June 2016.

facts.fact: A prefabricated second version, MFS II, won a Silver Lion at the 2016 Venice Architecture Biennale.
facts.quote: In 2016, a second iteration of the Makoko Floating School, called the Makoko Floating School II (MFS II), was unveiled at the Venice Architectural Biennale. This updated version was designed to be a prefabricated, rapid-assembly version of the original. It was awarded the Silver Lion prize, recognized as a “powerful demonstration, be it in Lagos in Venice, that architecture, at once iconic and pragmatic, can amplify the importance of education”.

facts.fact: The Royal Theatre of Rabat, formerly the Grand Theatre, is a performing arts centre on the left bank of the Bou Regreg, designed by Zaha Hadid with Zaha Hadid Architects.
facts.quote: The Royal Theatre of Rabat (French: Théâtre Royal de Rabat; Arabic: المسرح الملكي بالرباط), formerly known as the Grand Theatre of Rabat, is a performing arts center in Rabat, the capital of Morocco, located on the left bank of the Bou Regreg river. Designed by Zaha Hadid in collaboration with Zaha Hadid Architects, the building is one of the major cultural and architectural projects developed in Rabat in the 21st century.

facts.fact: Its form draws on the winding Bou Regreg river, Arabic calligraphy and Islamic and Moroccan architecture.
facts.quote: The overall composition draws inspiration from the winding course of the Bou Regreg and incorporates references to Arabic calligraphy and elements of Islamic architecture and Moroccan architectural traditions.

facts.fact: The main auditorium seats 1,821; a smaller theatre seats 170.
facts.quote: The main auditorium has a capacity of 1,821 seats and is designed to accommodate a range of theatrical, musical and other performing arts productions. The smaller theatre provides 170 seats in a seated configuration and can accommodate up to 250 people in a standing configuration.

facts.fact: An outdoor amphitheatre seats about 7,000.
facts.quote: An outdoor amphitheatre provides seating for approximately 7,000 spectators.

facts.fact: The main hall's faceted surfaces draw on Moroccan muqarnas.
facts.quote: The interior of the main auditorium features faceted surfaces that draw on the visual language of Moroccan muqarnas, while the circulation spaces connect the entrance, foyer, performance areas and ancillary facilities through a continuous sequence of interior spaces.

facts.fact: It is built of reinforced concrete and steel, with parts of the curved skin in glass-fibre reinforced concrete (GRC).
facts.quote: The structure incorporates reinforced concrete and steel, while sections of the external envelope use glass fiber reinforced concrete (GRC), allowing the construction of the building's complex geometries.

facts.fact: It was one of Hadid's last major designs; construction went on after her death in 2016 and was completed in 2021.
facts.quote: The Royal Theatre was among the last major projects designed by Zaha Hadid before her death in 2016. The project had already been conceived and was under development before her death, with construction continuing thereafter until its completion in 2021.

facts.fact: After years of delay it opened to the public on 22 April 2026.
facts.quote: The Royal Theatre opened to the public on 22 April 2026 during an inaugural artistic programme attended by Princesses Lalla Khadija, Lalla Meryem and Lalla Hasnaa, together with Brigitte Macron.

facts.fact: Carrières Centrales is a group of 1950s modernist housing in Casablanca designed by Georges Candilis, Shadrach Woods and Alexis Josic.
facts.quote: Carrières Centrales (Moroccan Arabic: كريان سنطرال) is a series of modernist housing developments in Casablanca, Morocco designed in the 1950s by architects Georges Candillis, Shadrach Woods, Alexis Josic.

facts.fact: It was the first project to test Michel Écochard's design, in Casablanca's Hay Mohammadi district.
facts.quote: Carrières Centrales, a site in the Hay Mohammadi district of Casablanca, was the first project to test Écochard's design.

facts.fact: Écochard's 8 × 8 m grid model was pioneering in collective housing.
facts.quote: Ecochard's 8x8 meter model, designed to address Casablanca's issues with overpopulation and rural exodus, was pioneering in the architecture of collective housing.

facts.fact: Influenced by Le Corbusier's Unité d'habitation and by communal slum life, the mid-rise blocks offered collective living with many balconies; residents named them Semiramis and Nid d'Abeille after the Hanging Gardens of Babylon and a honeycomb.
facts.quote: Influenced by Le Corbusier's Unité d'habitation and the communal nature of slum life, the resulting mid-rise complexes featured highly collective multilevel living exemplified by myriad balconies. The site's buildings became known by the residents as Semiramis and Nid D'Abeille as references to their visual similarities to honeycombs and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon respectively.

facts.fact: Sémiramis and Nid d'Abeille (Honeycomb) were among the first examples of 'vernacular modernism'.
facts.quote: Sémiramis, Nid d’Abeille (Honeycomb), and Carrières Centrales were some of the first examples of this Vernacular Modernism.

facts.fact: GAMMA's approach, shown at the 1953 CIAM, stressed local culture and climate alongside modernist principles.
facts.quote: He led the Groupe des Architectes Modernes Marocains (GAMMA), which revolutionized modernist architecture at the 1953 International Congress of Modern Architecture by emphasizing the importance of considering local culture and climate in addition to modernist architectural principles. This approach is called vernacular modernism.

facts.fact: Many residents have since altered the buildings, most often by walling in the balconies.
facts.quote: Since their construction, many of the complex's residents have modified the buildings significantly, most frequently by walling off the original balconies.

facts.fact: Krushi Bhawan, by Studio Lotus, is a building for the Government of Odisha's Department of Agriculture & Farmers' Empowerment, highly commended at the 2019 World Architecture Festival.
facts.quote: Krushi Bhawan, an official building for Government of Odisha's Department of Agriculture & Farmers' Empowerment. It was highly commended at the World Architecture Festival Awards in 2019.

facts.fact: Studio Lotus is a New Delhi design practice founded in 2002.
facts.quote: Studio Lotus is a multi-disciplinary design company, established in 2002, headquartered in New Delhi.

facts.fact: Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore is the home of the Pakistan Cricket Board and the national team, seating 27,000.
facts.quote: Gaddafi Stadium formerly known as Lahore Stadium, is a cricket stadium in Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan, owned by the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB). With a capacity of 27,000, it is the fourth largest cricket stadium of Pakistan. The headquarters of the Pakistan Cricket Board are situated at Gaddafi Stadium, thus making it the home of the Pakistan national cricket team.

facts.fact: It was designed by architect and engineer Nasreddin Murat-Khan and built in 1959 as Lahore Stadium.
facts.quote: Gaddafi stadium was built in 1959 and designed by architect and civil engineer Nasreddin Murat-Khan and construction was completed by Mian Abdul Khaliq and Company. It was originally established as the Lahore Stadium.

facts.fact: It was renamed after Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi on 19 March 1972.
facts.quote: On 19 March 1972, the stadium was renamed in honour of Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi by the then president of Pakistan, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto while addressing a public meeting in Lahore.

facts.fact: For the 1996 World Cup, Nayyar Ali Dada redesigned it with red hand-laid brickwork and arches, and replaced concrete benches with plastic seats.
facts.quote: In 1995–96, the Gaddafi Stadium was renovated by architect Nayyar Ali Dada, who was qualified from National College of Arts, for the 1996 Cricket World Cup. Dada's redesign was done with red, hand-laid brickwork and arches. Dada also had plastic seating installed in place of the existing concrete benches.

facts.fact: The space under the stands was enclosed for shops and offices, and the remodelled enclosures cut capacity from 65,250 to 27,000.
facts.quote: The lower portion under the stands was enclosed and converted to shops for boutiques and offices. Gaddafi Stadium, being the largest cricket stadium in Pakistan, used to have capacity of 65,250 spectators, until the redesigning of its enclosures reduced the capacity to 27,000.

facts.fact: It hosted the 1996 World Cup final, the first played in Pakistan.
facts.quote: The 1996 Cricket World Cup Final was held at Gaddafi Stadium, Lahore, Pakistan, on March 17, 1996. It was the first time a World Cup final was played in Pakistan, marking a historic moment for the country's cricketing legacy.

facts.fact: It was the first cricket ground in Pakistan with modern floodlights and their own standby generators.
facts.quote: It was the first cricket stadium in Pakistan to be equipped with modern floodlights with their own standby power generators.

facts.fact: Tecton was a group co-founded by Berthold Lubetkin and others in 1932 that led the bringing of continental modernism to Britain.
facts.quote: The Tecton Group was a radical architectural group co-founded by Berthold Lubetkin, Francis Skinner, Denys Lasdun, Michael Dugdale, Anthony Chitty, Val Harding, Godfrey Samuel, and Lindsay Drake in 1932 and disbanded in 1939. The group was one of the leaders in bringing continental modernism to Britain.

facts.fact: After its London Zoo work, Tecton designed Highpoint I, a block of flats in Highgate.
facts.quote: The group then designed the Highpoint I tower, an apartment complex in Highgate.

facts.fact: Though first meant for working-class residents, it set a new standard for luxury city living.
facts.quote: The complex set a new standard for luxury in city life, even though it was originally intended for working-class residents.

facts.fact: Built in 1935, it was an important experiment in high-rise housing and a key collaboration between engineer Ove Arup and Lubetkin, though Arup later said it had significant flaws.
facts.quote: Highpoint I, built in 1935, was an important experiment in high-rise residential design and one of Arup's most significant collaborations with Berthold Lubetkin. However, Arup later criticized the project, noting that it had significant flaws.

facts.fact: Tecton later built the even more luxurious Highpoint II on the neighbouring plot.
facts.quote: The group later designed the Highpoint II tower on an adjacent piece of land, which was even more luxurious than its predecessor.

facts.fact: The Penguin Pool at London Zoo was designed by Berthold Lubetkin and Tecton and built in 1934; Historic England calls it a key symbol of the Modern Movement.
facts.quote: The Penguin Pool at London Zoo, Regent's Park is a penguin enclosure designed in the International Modernist style by Berthold Lubetkin and the Tecton Group. Constructed in 1934, Historic England describe it as "a key symbol of British (and International) Modern Movement architecture".

facts.fact: It was highly experimental for its time, built entirely of reinforced concrete.
facts.quote: The pool was highly experimental for its time and place, being built entirely of reinforced concrete.

facts.fact: Around an elliptical pool, cantilevered interlocking spiral ramps cross the water seemingly without support, with a diving area, nesting boxes and a viewing gallery.
facts.quote: The structure has an elliptical pool at its centre, with "cantilevered interlocking spiral ramps", seemingly without support, crossing the centre of the pool, a glass-fronted diving area, and an enclosure with nesting boxes at one end. A viewing gallery runs around the exterior.

facts.fact: It is reinforced concrete finished in white cement render.
facts.quote: It is constructed of reinforced concrete and covered in white cement render.

facts.fact: Engineer Ove Arup made the spiral ramps possible by casting the concrete slabs as one element, with joints as strong as the spans.
facts.quote: Arup’s construction expertise in concrete was both critical and groundbreaking: arguing that concrete slabs, cast as one element with the joints as strong as the central spans, would enable architects to achieve any length and shape, he was instrumental in achieving the spiral ramps.

facts.fact: It was listed Grade I in 1970.
facts.quote: The pool had been listed by Historic England in 1970 as a Grade I listed structure, its highest possible grade reserved for buildings of "exceptional interest".

facts.fact: It housed penguins for 70 years and closed in 2004 over concerns for their welfare; it is now a water feature.
facts.quote: The pool housed the zoo's collection of penguins for 70 years. Changing attitudes to keeping animals in captivity, and concerns regarding the suitability of the structure for penguin well-being, saw the pool's closure in 2004 and its subsequent replacement by Penguin Beach. After a period of non-use, during which Lubetkin's daughter called for the structure to be "blown to smithereens", the pool was converted into a water feature.

facts.fact: St Peter's Seminary near Cardross is a former Roman Catholic seminary by Gillespie, Kidd & Coia that Docomomo calls a modern building of world significance.
facts.quote: St Peter's Seminary is a former Roman Catholic seminary near Cardross, Argyll and Bute, Scotland. Designed by the firm of Gillespie, Kidd & Coia, it has been described by the international architecture conservation organisation Docomomo International as a modern "building of world significance".

facts.fact: It is one of only 42 post-war buildings in Scotland listed at Category A.
facts.quote: It is one of only 42 post-war buildings in Scotland to be listed at Category A, the highest level of protection for a building of "special architectural or historic interest".

facts.fact: A new seminary was needed after a 1946 fire; talks with the architects began in 1953 and building started in 1961.
facts.quote: Following a fire in 1946 at St Peter's Seminary in the Glasgow suburb of Bearsden, a new home was needed for the seminary. Discussions began with Gillespie, Kidd & Coia in 1953, but the plans for a new college in the village of Cardross were not finalised until 1961, when building began.

facts.fact: Modernist and brutalist, and deeply indebted to Le Corbusier, it is widely seen as one of Scotland's most important modernist buildings.
facts.quote: Determinedly modernist, brutalist and owing a huge debt to Le Corbusier, the seminary is widely considered to be one of the most important examples of modernist architecture in Scotland.

facts.fact: The seminary closed in February 1980.
facts.quote: The seminary closed in February 1980.

facts.fact: Because of maintenance problems the modern buildings were not used after 1984, and vandalism began soon after.
facts.quote: Due to maintenance problems with the modern buildings, they were not used again after 1984, when the centre confined themselves to Kilmahew House, and vandalism began soon after.

facts.fact: It is regarded as Gillespie, Kidd & Coia's most significant work.
facts.quote: St. Peter's Seminary in Cardross, Argyll and Bute is regarded as Gillespie, Kidd & Coia's most significant work.

facts.fact: In July 2020 the site was given to the Kilmahew Education Trust, which plans to conserve it and bring back its educational use.
facts.quote: In July 2020, the site was given to the Kilmahew Education Trust Ltd who plan to reinstate the educational elements of the Seminary Complex after conservation and restoration.

facts.fact: The Royal Commonwealth Pool, one of Scotland's main swimming pools, is a Category A listed building in Edinburgh.
facts.quote: The Royal Commonwealth Pool is a category-A-listed building in St Leonard's, Edinburgh, Scotland that houses one of Scotland's main swimming pools.

facts.fact: It was commissioned in 1966 as part of the plan to bring the Commonwealth Games to Edinburgh.
facts.quote: The pool was commissioned by the Council under a plan by the then Lord Provost, Sir Herbert Archbold Brechin in 1966 as part of a wider project to bring the Commonwealth Games to Edinburgh.

facts.fact: Built 1967–69 by Robert Matthew Johnson-Marshall with structural input from Ove Arup & Partners, it hosted the aquatics of the 1970 Commonwealth Games.
facts.quote: Construction began in 1967 and was completed in October 1969. The architecture was by Robert Matthew Johnson Marshall with structural input from Ove Arup & Partners. The pool duly hosted the aquatic events at the 1970 British Commonwealth Games.

facts.fact: In 1993 Docomomo chose it as one of sixty key Scottish monuments of the post-war period.
facts.quote: In 1993 it was selected by the international conservation organisation DoCoMoMo as one of sixty key Scottish monuments of the post-war period.

facts.fact: A £37 million refurbishment by S&P Architects, 2009–2012, added new diving and teaching pools.
facts.quote: The project, led by Frank and Charlie of S&P Architects (now Space&Place Architects) began in August 2009, costing approximately £37 million, and included new 25 metres (82 ft) diving and teaching pools as well as improvements to the changing rooms, café, reception, and the dive gym. It was originally expected to be finished by mid-2011 but did not reopen until March 2012.

facts.fact: The refurbishment won the 2012 Scottish Design Award for best reuse of a listed building.
facts.quote: S&P Architects were the architects and lead consultants for the 2012 refurbishment and were awarded the Scottish Design Award in 2012 for the best reuse of a listed building.

facts.fact: Van der Vlugt's list of works dates the Sonneveld House in Rotterdam to 1933–34.
facts.quote: Sonneveld House in Rotterdam, 1933–34

facts.fact: Van Nelle directors, including Bertus Sonneveld, were so impressed by Van der Vlugt's factory that they commissioned him to design their own houses; the renovated Sonneveld House is now a museum with over 30,000 visitors a year.
facts.quote: Van der Leeuw and both company directors, Matthijs de Bruyn and Bertus Sonneveld, were so impressed by the skills of Van der Vlugt that they commissioned him to design and build private houses for themselves in Rotterdam and nearby Schiedam between 1928 and 1932. The fully renovated Sonneveld House is now a museum in the center of Rotterdam, with more than 30,000 annual visitors from all over the world.

facts.fact: The Brinkman & Van der Vlugt office lasted only about ten years, ending with Van der Vlugt's death in 1936.
facts.quote: The activities of the Brinkman & Van der Vlugt office lasted only about ten years because Leendert van der Vlugt has died in 1936 (Hodgkin's disease).

facts.fact: Mendelsohn's Schocken department store in Chemnitz (1927–1930) is known for its arched front with horizontal strips of windows.
facts.quote: Schocken department store, Chemnitz (1927-1930), known for its arched front with horizontal strips of windows.

facts.fact: Salman Schocken commissioned Mendelsohn for modernist stores in Nuremberg, Stuttgart and Chemnitz; the Chemnitz store, opened in 1930, is the only one to survive.
facts.quote: Schocken commissioned German Jewish architect Erich Mendelsohn to design Modernist style buildings. He opened branches in Nuremberg (1926), Stuttgart (1928) and Chemnitz (1930, the only one to survive).

facts.fact: Mendelsohn's shops, above all the Schocken stores, captured the consumer culture of the Weimar Republic.
facts.quote: Mendelsohn's work encapsulated the consumerism of the Weimar Republic, most particularly in his shops: most famously the Schocken Department Stores.

facts.fact: Mendelsohn developed a 'dynamic functionalism' in his department stores and cinemas.
facts.quote: Erich Mendelsohn (German pronunciation: [ˈeːʁɪç ˈmɛndl̩ˌzoːn] ; 21 March 1887 – 15 September 1953) was a German-British architect, known for his expressionist architecture in the 1920s, as well as for developing a dynamic functionalism in his projects for department stores and cinemas.

facts.fact: By 1930 the Schocken chain, with 20 stores, was one of the largest in Europe.
facts.quote: By 1930 the Schocken chain was one of the largest in Europe, with 20 stores.

facts.fact: Bohuslav Fuchs's list of Brno works dates Hotel Avion to 1927.

facts.fact: Hotel Avion houses a museum of functionalism and of Fuchs's life and work.
facts.quote: Hotel Avion in Brno, which is one of Fuchs' works, houses a museum of functionalism and life and work of Bohuslav Fuchs.

facts.fact: Fuchs is considered one of the most important Czech architects of the 20th century; his work is mainly in Brno.
facts.quote: He is considered one of the most important Czech architects of the 20th century. His work is primarily associated with the city of Brno.

facts.fact: Ernst Wiesner's Villa Stiassni in Brno dates from 1927–1929.
facts.quote: Vila Stiassni 1927 - 1929

facts.fact: Wiesner, one of interwar Brno's foremost architects, was strongly influenced by Adolf Loos.
facts.quote: His work was greatly influenced by Adolf Loos and his pure constructions with their classicized balance and monumentality are amongst the best works constructed in Brno at that time.

facts.fact: Built 1931–1933 in the Art Deco style for the British Prudential insurance company, it was the tallest building in interwar Poland.
facts.quote: Built between 1931 and 1933 in the Art Deco style, it served as a base for the British Prudential Insurance Company. It was the tallest building in interwar Poland.

facts.fact: The 18-storey, 66 m steel-framed tower was then the fourth-tallest skyscraper in Europe and Warsaw's tallest building until 1955.
facts.quote: At the time of its construction, the 18-story, 66 m Prudential House was the fourth-tallest skyscraper in Europe, after Ullsteinhaus, Telefónica Building and Boerentoren (the tallest). Built using a steel framework, it was the tallest building in Warsaw until the Palace of Culture and Science was completed in 1955.

facts.fact: Marcin Weinfeld designed it with offices below and luxury flats above; Stefan Bryła and Wenczesław Poniż designed its innovative steel frame.
facts.quote: Designed by Marcin Weinfeld, the Prudential House included office space on the lower stories and luxury apartments further up. The steel framework, which was innovative at the time, was designed by Stefan Bryła and Wenczesław Poniż.

facts.fact: In the 1944 Warsaw Uprising it was hit by about 1,000 shells, leaving only the bent steel frame standing.
facts.quote: The structure was heavily damaged during World War II, particularly during the Warsaw Uprising, when it was hit by approximately 1,000 artillery shells, including a 2-tonne Karl-Gerät mortar shell, leaving only the steel framework standing. The artillery damage bent the tower sideways, but it survived the war and was featured on numerous anti-war posters.

facts.fact: After the war Weinfeld himself adapted it as a hotel, its style changed from early modernism to socialist realism.
facts.quote: The tower was repaired after the war and turned into a hotel, and its design style was adapted from early modernism to socialist realism. The building's original architect, Marcin Weinfeld, adapted the building to its new role as a hotel.

facts.fact: A refurbishment restored the pre-war Art Deco facade and rebuilt the interior; it reopened as a five-star hotel in November 2018.
facts.quote: The façade was returned to its pre-war art deco form, while the socialist-realist interior was completely gutted and rebuilt in a contemporary style. In November 2018, the 142-room Hotel Warszawa reopened as a five-star hotel.

facts.fact: In 1936 Janusz Groszkowski put a 27 m antenna on the roof and began Europe's first television broadcasts from the building.
facts.quote: In 1936, a 27-meter antenna was constructed on the roof by professor Janusz Groszkowski, who started the first television broadcasts in Europe from the facility.

facts.fact: Kaunas Central Post Office is a former postal headquarters and one of the most notable buildings from Kaunas's time as Lithuania's temporary capital.
facts.quote: Kaunas Central Post Office (Lithuanian: Kauno centrinis paštas) is a former post office headquarters in Kaunas, Lithuania, which is one of the most notable buildings from the period when Kaunas was the temporary capital of Lithuania.

facts.fact: It stands on Laisvės alėja, was completed in 1931 to a design by Feliksas Vizbaras, and mixes functionalism with national decoration, becoming a model of Kaunas modernism.
facts.quote: The most prominent example is the Kaunas Central Post Office on Laisvės alėja, completed in 1931 to a design by Vizbaras. Combining functionalism with national decorative style and introducing numerous innovative solutions, it became a model of Kaunas modernism.

facts.fact: It is an example of the innovative use of curved glass for windows.
facts.quote: In particularly innovative projects, curved glass was used for windows, as in the Kaunas Central Post Office.

facts.fact: It is among the notable buildings of Kaunas modernism, several of which were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2023.
facts.quote: Notable examples of Kaunas modernism include the Kaunas Garrison Officers' Club Building, the Kaunas Central Post Office, the Church of the Resurrection of Christ, the Vytautas the Great War Museum, among others. Several of these buildings were awarded the European Heritage Label in 2015, and in 2023 they were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

facts.fact: Feliksas Vizbaras, educated in Riga, was one of the key architects of the Kaunas modernist style.
facts.quote: Among the key architects who shaped this style were Feliksas Vizbaras (1880–1966), educated in Riga; Vytautas Landsbergis-Žemkalnis (1893–1993), educated in Rome; and Edmundas Alfonsas Frykas, trained in Saint Petersburg.

facts.fact: Kaunas modernism often added motifs from Lithuanian textiles, woodcarving and folk painting to modernist facades and interiors.
facts.quote: National motifs and patterns derived from Lithuanian textiles, woodcarving, and folk painting were widely used in both façades and interiors.

facts.fact: The Resurrection Chapel in Turku cemetery (1941, finished in wartime) is one of Bryggman's two most famous works, a mature synthesis moving towards organic forms and a dialogue with the landscape.
facts.quote: His two most famous individual works are the extension to the library of Åbo Akademi University, Turku (1935), designed in a more strict Functionalism style, and the Resurrection Chapel (1941, completed during the wartime) in the Turku cemetery, which represents a mature synthesis of Bryggman's architecture, moving towards organic forms, and creating a dialogue with the surrounding landscape.

facts.fact: Its design and construction ran from 1938 to 1941.
facts.quote: Resurrection Chapel, Turku (1938-1941)

facts.fact: On the strength of the chapel, Bryggman was asked after the war to design many war memorials and cemetery chapels.
facts.quote: On the basis of the Resurrection Chapel design, Bryggman was commissioned after the war to design numerous war memorials and cemetery chapels, most notably the chapels at Lappeenranta, Lohja and Honkanummi in Vantaa.

facts.fact: Bryggman's architecture combines Nordic, classical and modernist qualities.
facts.quote: Bryggman's architecture is noted for its combination of Nordic, classical and modernist characteristics.

facts.fact: Aalto designed the Turun Sanomat Building in 1929–30, while the Viipuri Library was under way.
facts.quote: During that time, Aalto designed the Standard Apartment Building (1928–29) in Turku, the Turun Sanomat Building (1929–30), and the Paimio Sanatorium (1929–32), which he designed in collaboration with his first wife Aino Aalto.

facts.fact: Its cutting-edge, Le Corbusier-inspired language was one of the factors in Aalto's move to modernism.
facts.quote: A number of factors contributed to Aalto's shift towards modernism: his increased familiarity with international trends, facilitated by his travels throughout Europe; the opportunity to experiment with concrete prefabrication in the Standard Apartment Building; the cutting-edge Le Corbusier-inspired formal language of the Turun Sanomat Building; and Aalto's application of both in the Paimio Sanatorium and in the ongoing design for the library.

facts.fact: With Paimio, it is one of Aalto's comparatively pure modernist works, yet it already hints at his later move away from orthodox modernism.
facts.quote: Although the Turun Sanomat Building and Paimio Sanatorium are comparatively pure modernist works, they carried the seeds of his questioning of such an orthodox modernist approach and a move to a more daring, synthetic attitude.

facts.fact: Turun Sanomat, the client, is the leading regional newspaper of Southwest Finland, published in Turku.
facts.quote: Turun Sanomat is the leading regional newspaper of the region of Southwest Finland. It is published in the region's capital, Turku and the third most widely read morning newspaper in Finland after Helsingin Sanomat and Aamulehti.

facts.fact: Sunila's pulp mill, run by the Ahlström group, opened in 1938 on the site of an earlier sawmill.
facts.quote: In 1938, a pulp mill was opened there on the site of an earlier sawmill, operated by the Ahlström paper and pulp manufacturing group through its subsidiary Sunila Oy.

facts.fact: Alvar and Aino Aalto were commissioned on the suggestion of Ahlström's chief executive Harry Gullichsen.
facts.quote: The design for the factory complex was commissioned from the Finnish architect couple Alvar and Aino Aalto, on the suggestion of the Ahlström chief executive at the time, the industrialist Harry Gullichsen.

facts.fact: Aalto's list of works gives the pulp mill, housing and town plan as 1936–1939.
facts.quote: 1936–1939: Ahlstrom Sunila Pulp Mill, Housing, and Town Plan, Kotka, Finland

facts.fact: Over 20 staff housing buildings, mostly low-rise flats and terraces, were built mainly to Aalto's design from the mid-1930s to the mid-1950s.
facts.quote: To accommodate the factory staff, an adjacent residential estate was built, also designed mainly by Aalto. The estate comprises over 20 buildings, mostly low-rise apartment blocks, as well as terraced houses and a detached house serving as the factory manager's residence, 'Kantola', which was the first of the residential buildings to be completed. The buildings were constructed over two decades from mid-1930s to mid-1950s.

facts.fact: The housing sits in woodland, shaped to the land's contours for residents' health and well-being.
facts.quote: The residential buildings are located in a natural wooded area, intended to promote the health and well-being of the residents, and were designed to fit in with the nature and the contours of the land.

facts.fact: Sunila is the largest Aalto-designed whole ever built.
facts.quote: The Sunila area is the largest Aalto-designed entity ever built.

facts.fact: It is in the Docomomo register (1993) and became part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing of Aalto's works in July 2026.
facts.quote: In 1993, the site was included in the DOCOMOMO modern architecture register. In 2025, Finland proposed Sunila to be added to the UNESCO World Heritage Sites collection as part of 13 Aalto-designed sites. UNESCO designated the Aalto Works as a World Heritage Site in July 2026.

facts.fact: Still working, it is the oldest surviving sulfate pulp mill in Finland.
facts.quote: Since 2009 part of the Stora Enso group, the Sunila plant remains in operation as the oldest surviving sulfate pulp mill in Finland.

facts.fact: The Sanatorium Joseph Lemaire (1937), in Tombeek, Overijse, is a modern building by architect Maxime Brunfaut.
facts.quote: Also in Tombeek, the Sanatorium Joseph Lemaire (1937), a modern building from architect Maxime Brunfaut.
